worked.title: An exponential growth model
worked.problem: An account starts at $500 and grows 4% per year: f(x) = 500(1.04)^x. How much is in it after 5 years?

worked.title: A linear-quadratic system

worked.title: A system from a word problem
worked.problem: One gym charges a $30 joining fee plus $20 per month. Another has no joining fee and charges $26 per month. After how many months is the total cost the same?
steps: Write each cost as a function of months x: y = 20x + 30 and y = 26x.
Set them equal: 20x + 30 = 26x, so 30 = 6x and x = 5.
Substitute back: y = 26(5) = 130. Check the other gym: 20(5) + 30 = 130.
On the graph the two lines cross at (5, 130).
worked.answer: After 5 months both gyms cost $130 in total.

worked.title: A parameter that gives exactly one solution
worked.problem: For which value of k does kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 have exactly one real solution (k is not 0)?
steps: A quadratic has exactly one real solution when its discriminant is zero: b² − 4ac = 0.
Here a = k, b = 4, c = 1, so 16 − 4k = 0.
Solve: k = 4.
Check: 4x² + 4x + 1 = (2x + 1)², which touches the x-axis once, at x = −1/2.
worked.answer: k = 4. Drag k to 4 on the graph and the parabola just touches the x-axis.

worked.title: Where a line meets a circle
worked.problem: At which points does the line y = x + 1 cross the circle x² + y² = 25?
steps: Substitute y = x + 1: x² + (x + 1)² = 25.
Expand: 2x² + 2x + 1 = 25, so 2x² + 2x − 24 = 0, which is x² + x − 12 = 0.
Factor: (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0, so x = −4 or x = 3.
Find y with y = x + 1: y = −3 and y = 4.
worked.answer: The points are (−4, −3) and (3, 4). Both satisfy x² + y² = 25: 16 + 9 = 25 and 9 + 16 = 25.

worked.title: Amplitude and period of a sine wave
worked.problem: What are the amplitude and the period of y = 3 sin(2x)?
steps: For y = a sin(bx), the amplitude is |a|, so the amplitude is 3.
The period is 2π/b = 2π/2 = π radians.
In degrees the same period is 360°/2 = 180°. Switch the calculator to DEG to see one cycle every 180.
worked.answer: Amplitude 3 and period π (180°). The graph reaches its first maximum at x = π/4.

worked.title: Check a quadratic you solved by hand
worked.problem: You found that f(x) = x² − 6x + 5 has roots 1 and 5 and a vertex at (3, −4). Is that right?

worked.title: Intercepts and end behavior of an exponential
worked.problem: For f(x) = 2^x − 4, find the intercepts and describe what happens as x becomes very negative.
steps: y-intercept: f(0) = 2⁰ − 4 = 1 − 4 = −3.
x-intercept: set 2^x − 4 = 0, so 2^x = 4 and x = 2.
As x gets very negative, 2^x gets close to 0, so f(x) gets close to −4. The line y = −4 is a horizontal asymptote.
worked.answer: y-intercept (0, −3), x-intercept (2, 0), and the graph levels off at y = −4 on the left.

worked.title: A system of inequalities
worked.problem: Describe the solution region of y > x + 2 and y < −2x + 5.
steps: Find where the boundary lines meet: x + 2 = −2x + 5, so 3x = 3 and x = 1, giving the point (1, 3).
Test (0, 3): 3 > 0 + 2 is true and 3 < 5 is true, so (0, 3) is in the region.
Test (0, 0): 0 > 2 is false, so the origin is not in the region.
Both boundaries are dashed because the inequalities are strict.
worked.answer: The region is above y = x + 2 and below y = −2x + 5, opening to the left of the corner (1, 3). The corner itself is not included.

worked.title: Find a maximum, then confirm it with the derivative
worked.problem: Find the maximum value of f(x) = x²e^(−x) for x ≥ 0.
steps: Use the product rule: f′(x) = 2x·e^(−x) − x²·e^(−x) = x(2 − x)e^(−x).
Set f′(x) = 0: x = 0 or x = 2. Since e^(−x) is always positive, the sign of f′ is the sign of x(2 − x).
f′ is positive for 0 < x < 2 and negative for x > 2, so f has a maximum at x = 2.
worked.answer: The maximum is 4e^(−2) ≈ 0.541 at x = 2. The Key points list shows the same point. On the exam, show the sign analysis rather than citing the graph.

worked.title: A definite integral with a clean antiderivative
worked.problem: Evaluate the integral of x²e^(−x) from 0 to 2.
steps: An antiderivative is F(x) = −e^(−x)(x² + 2x + 2); differentiate it to confirm that F′(x) = x²e^(−x).
worked.answer: The area is 2 − 10e^(−2) ≈ 0.647. Shade it with int(x^2*exp(-x), 0, 2) to check the value.

sources: College Board: AP Exams calculator policy

pages.desc: Find the domain and range from a graph. Plot any function, see where it exists and read restrictions quickly with this free online grapher.
intro: Domain and range questions ask two different things about the same curve: which x-values are allowed, and which y-values actually show up. Reading both off a picture is far quicker than testing numbers one by one. Look for a left edge where a square root starts, a gap where a denominator hits zero, or a floor and ceiling that the curve never crosses.

Plot your function here and trace the edges. Horizontal extent gives the domain, vertical extent gives the range, and any open gap tells you which single value to exclude. Then confirm the algebra: a radicand must be nonnegative, a denominator must not be zero, and a logarithm needs a positive input. Writing the answer in interval notation or set notation is much easier once you have seen the shape.
points: Domain is the set of inputs, so scan left to right and note where the curve begins, ends, or breaks.
Range is the set of outputs, so scan bottom to top and find the lowest and highest heights the curve reaches.
A square root, a fraction and a logarithm each place a different restriction on x; check them one at a time.
A curve that heads off the screen forever in one direction means that end of the interval is infinity, not a visible edge.

examples.l: Starts at (-4, 0): domain x ≥ -4, range y ≥ 0
Breaks at x = 2: domain is all x except 2, range is all y except 0
Upper half of a circle: domain -3 ≤ x ≤ 3, range 0 ≤ y ≤ 3

faq.q: What is the difference between domain and range?
faq.a: Domain lists every input x the function accepts. Range lists every output y it can produce. A function like y = x² accepts any x, yet its outputs never go below 0.

faq.q: How do I find the domain of a fraction?
faq.a: Set the denominator equal to zero and solve. Those x-values are excluded. For 1/(x - 2), the denominator is zero at x = 2, so the domain is every real number except 2.

faq.q: Why does a square root limit the domain?
faq.a: Real square roots only exist for nonnegative numbers. For sqrt(x + 4), you need x + 4 ≥ 0, which gives x ≥ -4. The graph confirms it by starting at x = -4.

faq.q: How can the graph show the range of a parabola?
faq.a: Find the vertex. If the parabola opens up, the vertex y-value is the minimum and the range starts there. If it opens down, the vertex y-value is the maximum.

faq.q: Does a hole in the graph change the domain?
faq.a: Yes. A removed point at one x-value means that x is not in the domain, even though the curve looks continuous around it. Zoom in near the suspect x-value to check.

how: Type something like sqrt(x + 4) or 1/(x - 2) into the first row. Use sqrt() for roots and a slash for fractions.
Drag the graph sideways and mark where the curve first appears and where it stops. Those marks are your domain endpoints.
Now ignore x and look only at height. The lowest and highest y-values the curve reaches are your range endpoints.
Zoom in around any x-value that makes a denominator zero. A break there means you must exclude that value from the domain.
Use brackets for included endpoints and parentheses for excluded ones, for example [-4, ∞) for sqrt(x + 4).

worked.title: Domain and range of a square root
worked.problem: Find the domain and range of f(x) = sqrt(x + 4).
steps: The expression under the root cannot be negative, so x + 4 >= 0 and x >= -4.
The smallest output is sqrt(0) = 0 at x = -4, and the outputs keep growing without limit.
On the graph the curve starts at (-4, 0) and rises to the right.
worked.answer: Domain: x >= -4. Range: y >= 0.

worked.title: Domain and range of a rational function
worked.problem: Find the domain and range of g(x) = 1/(x - 2).
steps: Division by zero is undefined, so x - 2 cannot be 0. Exclude x = 2.
The fraction can never equal 0, so y = 0 is not in the range.
The graph has a vertical asymptote at x = 2 and a horizontal asymptote at y = 0.
worked.answer: Domain: all real x except 2. Range: all real y except 0.

pages.title: Linear Equation Grapher: Slope & Intercepts | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph any linear equation and see its slope, x-intercept and y-intercept instantly. A free online line grapher for algebra homework and tests.
intro: A linear equation produces a straight line, and two numbers decide everything about it: the slope, which says how steep and in which direction, and the y-intercept, which says where it crosses the vertical axis. Plotting the line lets you check both at a glance instead of trusting a hand sketch. Positive slope climbs to the right, negative slope falls, and a slope of zero is perfectly flat.

Use this grapher to compare lines side by side. Parallel lines share a slope, perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals, and two lines with different slopes cross exactly once. The root, where the line meets the x-axis, is listed under Key points, which is handy for checking the solution to an equation like 2x - 3 = 0 without any algebra.
points: Slope is rise over run: a slope of 2 means up 2 for every 1 step right.
The y-intercept is the value at x = 0, and the x-intercept (root) is where y = 0.
Parallel lines never meet because their slopes match; perpendicular slopes multiply to -1.
A vertical line has no slope and is not a function, so it is written as x = a number.

examples.l: Slope 2, y-intercept -3, crosses the x-axis at 1.5
Falling line with root at x = 8
Slope -1/2 is perpendicular to the slope-2 line above; graph both and compare the angle

faq.q: How do I find the slope from a graph?
faq.a: Pick two clear points on the line, subtract the y-values, then divide by the difference in x-values. On a rising line the answer is positive, on a falling line it is negative.

faq.q: What does a slope of zero look like?
faq.a: A flat horizontal line, such as y = 3. Every x gives the same y, so the line never rises or falls.

faq.q: How can I tell if two lines are parallel?
faq.a: Graph both. If they never cross and run at the same angle, their slopes are equal. Compare the equations too: matching slopes with different intercepts means parallel.

faq.q: Where do two lines intersect?
faq.a: Add both equations in separate rows. The crossing point is marked and listed under Key points with its x and y coordinates.

faq.q: Can I graph a vertical line here?
faq.a: Type x = 4 as an equation. Vertical lines are not functions of x, so they are drawn as an implicit curve rather than a y = form.

how: Enter y in terms of x, such as 2x - 3 or -0.5x + 4. The graph appears as you type, with no button to press.
Open Key points to see the y-intercept and the root. Tap an entry and the plot jumps to that location.
Tap + and type another equation. Compare slopes by eye, then check whether the lines are parallel, perpendicular or crossing.
Trace two points on the line and compute rise over run. It should match the coefficient in front of x.
Zoom out for the big picture.
Pinch or scroll to see where far-apart lines eventually meet. The home button restores the default view.

worked.title: Slope and intercepts from an equation
worked.problem: Graph y = 2x - 3 and find its slope and intercepts.
steps: In y = mx + b the slope is m = 2 and the y-intercept is b = -3, so the line crosses the y-axis at (0, -3).
For the x-intercept set y = 0: 2x - 3 = 0, so x = 1.5.
Plot (0, -3), then rise 2 and run 1 to reach (1, -1).
worked.answer: Slope 2, y-intercept (0, -3), x-intercept (1.5, 0).

worked.title: Equation of a line through two points
worked.problem: Find the line through (1, 2) and (4, 8).
steps: Substitute (1, 2) into y = 2x + b: 2 = 2 + b, so b = 0.
worked.answer: y = 2x.

pages.title: System of Equations Grapher & Solver | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Solve a system of equations by graphing. Plot two or more equations and see the intersection point marked automatically, free and online.
intro: Solving a system by graphing means finding where two curves meet. Each equation draws its own curve, and any point that sits on both is a solution to the whole system. This is the visual twin of substitution and elimination, and it works for lines, parabolas and other functions alike, not only for neat linear pairs.

Enter each equation in its own row and watch the crossings. Two lines can intersect once, never (parallel), or everywhere (the same line). A line and a parabola can cross twice, touch once, or miss entirely. The intersection points are labeled in Key points with coordinates, so you can compare them with the answer you found by algebra and catch a sign error before it costs you marks.
points: A solution of the system is any point lying on every curve at once.
Parallel lines mean no solution; identical lines mean infinitely many.
A line and a parabola can give zero, one or two intersection points.
Solve both equations for y first so they can be typed as y = expressions.

examples.l: Add x + 1 as a second row: the lines cross at (2, 3)
Add x + 2 as a second row: crossings at (-2, 0) and (3, 5)
Add 2x - 3 as a second row: parallel lines, so no intersection

faq.q: How do I solve a system of equations by graphing?
faq.a: Graph both equations, then read the coordinates of the point where they cross. Check it by substituting x and y into both original equations.

faq.q: What if the lines never cross?
faq.a: Then the system has no solution. The lines are parallel, which means the slopes match but the intercepts differ.

faq.q: Can I solve a nonlinear system this way?
faq.a: Yes. Graph a parabola, circle or exponential next to a line. Every crossing is a solution, and the Key points list gives their coordinates.

faq.q: Why is my intersection not exactly a whole number?
faq.a: Many systems have decimal or fractional answers. The marked point shows several decimal places, which you can compare with an exact fraction from algebra.

faq.q: How do I rewrite an equation to enter it?
faq.a: Isolate y. For 2x + y = 7, subtract 2x from both sides to get y = 7 - 2x, then type 7 - 2x.

how: Solve each equation for y so the first becomes, say, 7 - 2x and the second x + 1.
Type the first equation, tap +, and type the second. Each gets its own color on the plot.
Look for the point where the curves meet, then open Key points to read its exact coordinates.
No crossing, one crossing or several. Zoom out in case a second intersection is hiding off screen.
Plug the x and y values back into both original equations. If both sides match each time, the solution is correct.

worked.title: A line and a parabola
worked.problem: Solve y = x^2 - 4 and y = x + 2.
steps: Set the right sides equal: x^2 - 4 = x + 2, so x^2 - x - 6 = 0.
Factor: (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 3 or x = -2.
worked.answer: Two solutions: (3, 5) and (-2, 0). They are the two intersection points on the graph.

worked.title: Two lines
worked.problem: Solve y = 2x + 1 and y = -x + 7.
steps: Set 2x + 1 = -x + 7, so 3x = 6 and x = 2.
Substitute: y = 2(2) + 1 = 5.
Check in the second equation: -2 + 7 = 5.
worked.answer: The lines meet at (2, 5).

pages.title: Graphing Inequalities Calculator Online | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph linear and quadratic inequalities with shaded regions. A free online inequality grapher that shows solid or dashed boundaries clearly.
intro: An inequality describes a whole region of the plane rather than a single curve. The boundary is the equation with the inequality sign swapped for an equals sign, and the shading marks every point that makes the statement true. Getting the boundary style and the shaded side right are the two details that graders look for first.

Type an inequality such as y > 2x + 1 and the plot draws the boundary and shades the correct side. Strict signs (> and <) give a dashed boundary because points on the line are not included, while ≥ and ≤ give a solid one. If you want to double-check by hand, pick a test point such as the origin, substitute it, and see whether the shading agrees. Parabolas, absolute values and circles can serve as boundaries too.
points: A dashed boundary means the line itself is not part of the solution; a solid one means it is.
y greater than the boundary shades above it, and y less than shades below.
Test a point like (0, 0) in the original inequality to confirm the shaded side.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips the inequality sign, so watch for it when isolating y.

examples.l: Dashed line, shaded above: points on the line do not count
Solid parabola, shaded below, so the inside region under the curve
Solid V-shaped boundary with everything above it shaded

faq.q: How do I know whether the line is solid or dashed?
faq.a: Look at the sign. Greater than or less than alone gives a dashed line. Greater than or equal to, or less than or equal to, gives a solid line.

faq.q: Which side should be shaded?
faq.a: Substitute a point not on the boundary, such as (0, 0). If the inequality is true there, shade that side; if false, shade the other.

faq.q: What happens when I divide by a negative?
faq.a: The inequality reverses. For -2y > 6 you get y < -3, so the shading is below the line y = -3, not above.

faq.q: Can I graph an inequality with x and y squared?
faq.a: Yes. Try x^2 + y^2 < 9 for the inside of a circle. The boundary is dashed because the sign is strict.

faq.q: Is this the same as graphing a system?
faq.a: A single inequality has one shaded region. A system overlaps several regions, which has its own page for combined constraints.

how: Enter it with y on the left, for example y > 2x + 1 or y <= x^2 - 3. Use <= and >= or the ≤ ≥ symbols.
A dashed edge means strict, a solid edge means inclusive. If that looks wrong, recheck your sign.
Pick a test point on the shaded side and substitute it into the inequality. It should come out true.
Replace the line with a parabola or abs(x) and see how the shaded region changes shape.
Pan and zoom to see where the region ends, which matters when a problem asks for the largest or smallest allowed value.

worked.title: Shade above a line
worked.problem: Graph y > 2x + 1 and decide whether (0, 0) is a solution.
steps: The boundary is the line y = 2x + 1. Because the sign is > (not >=), the line is dashed.
Test (0, 0): 0 > 2(0) + 1 is 0 > 1, which is false.
So shade the side that does not contain (0, 0): the region above the line.
worked.answer: Shade above the dashed line; (0, 0) is not a solution.

worked.title: Shade under a parabola
worked.problem: Graph y <= x^2 - 3 and test (0, -5).
steps: The boundary is the parabola y = x^2 - 3, drawn solid because of <=.
Test (0, -5): -5 <= 0 - 3 is -5 <= -3, which is true.
So the solution is the region below and on the parabola.
worked.answer: Shade below the solid parabola; (0, -5) is a solution.

pages.title: Piecewise Function Grapher & Plotter | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Plot piecewise functions with a different rule on each interval. A free online grapher for step, absolute value and conditional definitions.
intro: A piecewise function uses different rules on different parts of the x-axis. Tax brackets, shipping fees and parking rates all work this way, and so do absolute value and step functions. The graph is the clearest way to see where one rule hands off to the next, and whether the curve joins up smoothly or leaps.

Here you write the pieces with a conditional: condition ? value if true : value if false. For example, x < 0 ? -x : x^2 uses -x for negative inputs and x² otherwise. Chain a second conditional to add a third piece. Check each boundary carefully: a continuous function meets at the same height from both sides, a jump leaves a gap, and the choice between < and ≤ decides which side owns the boundary point.
points: Each piece applies only on its own interval, so the curve switches formula at the boundary.
Continuity at a boundary means both pieces give the same y-value there.
A jump discontinuity leaves a vertical gap between the two pieces.
Nest conditionals to add pieces: x < 3 ? a : x < 6 ? b : c.

examples.l: Both pieces equal 3 at x = 1, so the graph is continuous
Jumps up by 3 at x = 2: a jump discontinuity
Three flat steps, like a tiered fee schedule

faq.q: How do I type a piecewise function?
faq.a: Use condition ? then : else. Write x < 0 ? -x : x^2 to use -x when x is negative and x^2 otherwise. For more pieces, put another conditional in the else part.

faq.q: How can I tell if a piecewise function is continuous?
faq.a: Evaluate both formulas at the boundary x-value. If they agree, the pieces connect. If not, you will see a gap or a jump in the plot.

faq.q: What is the difference between < and ≤ at a boundary?
faq.a: It decides which piece owns the boundary point. With x < 2 the first piece stops just before 2, and the second piece takes the value at 2.

faq.q: Is the absolute value function piecewise?
faq.a: Yes. |x| equals -x for negative x and x for nonnegative x. That is why it graphs as a V with a corner at the origin.

faq.q: Can I combine conditions?
faq.a: Use && for and, and || for or. For instance, x > 0 && x < 4 ? x^2 : NaN draws a parabola only between 0 and 4.

how: Start with the condition and its formula: for example x < 1 ? 2*x + 1 and then a colon.
After the colon, type the rule for everything else, such as 4 - x. The graph updates as you type.
Zoom in on the switch point and compare the heights from the left and right.
Nest another conditional after the colon to create a third rule, then check the second boundary too.
Hide parts you do not want.
Use NaN as a value to leave a region empty, which is how domain restrictions are drawn.

worked.title: Evaluate a piecewise function
worked.problem: Let f(x) = -x for x < 0 and f(x) = x^2 for x >= 0. Find f(-3), f(0) and f(2).
steps: 0 is not less than 0, so use x^2: f(0) = 0.
worked.answer: f(-3) = 3, f(0) = 0, f(2) = 4. The two pieces meet at the origin, so the graph has no break.

worked.title: A jump discontinuity
worked.problem: Let f(x) = 2x + 1 for x < 1 and f(x) = 5 - x for x >= 1. Is f continuous at x = 1?
steps: Left of 1 the rule 2x + 1 approaches 3 as x approaches 1.
At x = 1 the second rule gives f(1) = 5 - 1 = 4.
The limit from the left (3) differs from f(1) = 4, so the graph jumps.
worked.answer: Not continuous at x = 1: there is a jump of 1.

pages.title: Rational Function Grapher: Asymptotes & Holes | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph rational functions and see vertical asymptotes, horizontal asymptotes and holes clearly. Free online tool for precalculus and AP prep.
intro: A rational function is one polynomial divided by another, and its graph is full of features that are easy to miss when you only plug in numbers. Where the denominator is zero, the curve either shoots off along a vertical asymptote or leaves a single missing point called a hole. Far from the origin, it settles toward a horizontal or slant line that depends on the degrees of the top and bottom.

Plot your fraction and factor it first. A factor that cancels from both numerator and denominator creates a hole; a factor that remains in the denominator creates an asymptote. The zeros of the numerator are the x-intercepts. The default example, (x² - 1)/(x - 2), has a vertical asymptote at x = 2 and bends toward the slant line y = x + 2, because the top is one degree higher than the bottom.
points: Zeros of the numerator that do not cancel give the x-intercepts.
A cancelled factor leaves a hole; an uncancelled denominator factor leaves a vertical asymptote.
Equal degrees on top and bottom give a horizontal asymptote at the ratio of leading coefficients.
One degree more on top gives a slant asymptote found by polynomial division.

examples.l: Factor and cancel: a hole at (2, 4) and otherwise the line y = x + 2
Vertical asymptotes at x = -1 and x = 1, horizontal asymptote y = 0
No vertical asymptote and a horizontal asymptote at y = 2

faq.q: How do I find the vertical asymptote of a rational function?
faq.a: Factor the denominator, cancel any factors shared with the numerator, then set each remaining factor to zero. Each solution is a vertical asymptote.

faq.q: What is a hole in a graph?
faq.a: It is a single missing point where a factor cancelled from the top and bottom. The curve looks continuous but the function is undefined at that x.

faq.q: When is there a slant asymptote?
faq.a: When the numerator's degree is exactly one more than the denominator's. Divide the polynomials; the quotient, ignoring the remainder, is the slant line.

faq.q: How do I find the horizontal asymptote?
faq.a: Compare degrees. Smaller top degree gives y = 0. Equal degrees give y equal to the ratio of the leading coefficients. A larger top degree gives none.

faq.q: Why can the curve cross a horizontal asymptote?
faq.a: Asymptotes describe end behavior, not every x. Near the middle the graph may cross the line, but for very large |x| it settles toward it.

how: Put parentheses around the top and bottom, as in (x^2 - 1)/(x - 2), so the division applies to the whole expression.
Look for places where the curve goes vertical or a point is missing, then match them to zeros of the denominator.
Zoom far out left and right to see which line the curve approaches.
Open Key points for the y-intercept and any roots, which come from the numerator.
Type a factored version, like (x - 1)(x + 1)/(x - 2), and confirm it draws the same picture.

worked.title: Asymptotes and intercepts
worked.problem: Analyze f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 2).
steps: The denominator is 0 at x = 2, and the numerator is 3 there, so x = 2 is a vertical asymptote.
The numerator is 0 at x = -1 and x = 1: these are the x-intercepts. The y-intercept is f(0) = -1/-2 = 0.5.
Divide: x^2 - 1 = (x - 2)(x + 2) + 3, so f(x) = x + 2 + 3/(x - 2). The slant asymptote is y = x + 2.
worked.answer: Vertical asymptote x = 2, slant asymptote y = x + 2, intercepts (-1, 0), (1, 0) and (0, 0.5).

worked.title: A hole instead of an asymptote
steps: Factor the numerator: (x - 3)(x + 3).
Cancel the common factor (x - 3): h(x) = x + 3 for x not equal to 3.
The cancelled factor leaves a hole at x = 3, where y = 3 + 3 = 6.
worked.answer: A line y = x + 3 with a hole at (3, 6); no vertical asymptote.

pages.title: Square Root Function Grapher | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph square root functions and their transformations online. See the starting point, domain and range change as you shift, stretch and reflect.
intro: The square root function is half of a sideways parabola, so its graph starts at a corner and bends gently upward and to the right. That starting point is the key feature. For y = sqrt(x - h) + k the corner sits at (h, k), and the curve exists only to one side of it because you cannot take the real square root of a negative number.

Experiment with shifts, flips and stretches. A number outside the root moves or stretches the curve vertically, while a number inside shifts it horizontally, with the sign working opposite to what you might guess. A negative sign in front flips the graph downward, and a negative x inside flips it to the left. Because the growth slows as x increases, square root models appear in physics for things like fall time and pendulum length.
points: The starting point (h, k) is found by setting the inside of the root to zero.
The domain is every x that keeps the radicand nonnegative, so it is a half-line.
A negative multiplier outside reflects the curve below the x-axis.
The curve rises steeply at first and then flattens, unlike a line or a parabola.

examples.l: Starting point at (-3, -1): shifted left 3 and down 1
Flipped to the left; the curve exists only for x ≤ 2
Vertically stretched by 2 and starting at (1, 2)

faq.q: What is the domain of a square root function?
faq.a: Set the expression under the root to be at least zero and solve. For sqrt(x + 3), x + 3 ≥ 0 gives x ≥ -3.

faq.q: How do I find where the graph starts?
faq.a: Set the radicand equal to zero to get the x-coordinate, then evaluate the whole function there. The result is the starting point.

faq.q: Why does adding inside the root move the graph left?
faq.a: Because sqrt(x + 3) reaches zero at x = -3, not at +3. Inside changes move the graph opposite to the sign you see.

faq.q: How is sqrt(x) related to x²?
faq.a: They are inverses on x ≥ 0. Reflect the half-parabola x² across the line y = x and you get the square root curve.

faq.q: Can the output be negative?
faq.a: Only if you put a negative sign outside, as in -sqrt(x). The root itself is never negative, so the range starts at the starting y-value and goes up or down from there.

how: Enter sqrt(x) or the shifted form, such as sqrt(x + 3) - 1. A square-root symbol on the keyboard works too.
Find the corner where the curve begins. Compare it with the numbers in your equation.
Add a minus sign in front of the root, then another inside beside x, and see the two different reflections.
Multiply by 2, then by 0.5, to watch the curve get steeper and then flatter.
Read the left end for the domain and the starting height for the range.

worked.title: Shifted square root
worked.problem: Graph f(x) = sqrt(x + 3) - 1 and find its starting point and intercepts.
steps: Shift left 3 and down 1: the curve starts at (-3, -1) and the domain is x >= -3.
x-intercept: sqrt(x + 3) = 1, so x + 3 = 1 and x = -2.
y-intercept: f(0) = sqrt(3) - 1, about 0.732.
worked.answer: Start (-3, -1); x-intercept (-2, 0); y-intercept about (0, 0.732).

worked.title: Reflected square root
worked.problem: Describe g(x) = -sqrt(x) and find g(9).
steps: The minus sign reflects sqrt(x) across the x-axis, so every output is 0 or negative.
Domain x >= 0, range y <= 0.
worked.answer: g(9) = -3; domain x >= 0, range y <= 0.

pages.title: Quadratic Graphing Calculator (Parabolas) | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph quadratics and parabolas with sliders. Find the vertex, roots and y-intercept automatically with this free online quadratic calculator.
intro: A quadratic in standard form, y = ax² + bx + c, draws a parabola, and the three coefficients each control something you can see. The sign of a decides whether it opens up or down, c is where it crosses the y-axis, and the combination of a and b locates the axis of symmetry at x = -b/(2a). The roots are where it meets the x-axis, and they are the solutions of ax² + bx + c = 0.

Graph a quadratic to learn how many real solutions it has before doing the algebra. Two crossings means two roots, a single touch means one repeated root, and no crossing means the discriminant b² - 4ac is negative. The default x² - 4x + 3 factors as (x - 1)(x - 3), so it crosses at 1 and 3, with its lowest point halfway between them at x = 2.
points: If a is positive the parabola opens up and has a minimum; if negative it opens down.
The axis of symmetry is x = -b/(2a), and the vertex sits on it.
The discriminant b² - 4ac tells you whether there are two, one or no real roots.
The roots are the x-intercepts, and the constant c is the y-intercept.

examples.l: Opens down, roots at 1 and 5, maximum at (3, 4)
Touches the x-axis once at x = -1: discriminant zero
Never reaches the x-axis: no real roots

faq.q: How do I find the vertex from standard form?
faq.a: Compute x = -b/(2a), then substitute it into the function to get y. For x² - 4x + 3, x = 2 and y = -1, so the vertex is (2, -1).

faq.q: What does the discriminant tell me?
faq.a: Positive means two real roots, zero means one repeated root, and negative means none. The graph shows the same thing as two, one or zero x-axis crossings.

faq.q: How can I solve a quadratic equation by graphing?
faq.a: Graph the quadratic and read the x-intercepts. They are listed under Key points as roots, and you can compare them with the quadratic formula.

faq.q: Why do some parabolas not touch the x-axis?
faq.a: Their vertex lies above the axis while opening up, or below it while opening down. The roots would be complex numbers, which a real graph cannot show.

faq.q: How is this different from vertex form?
faq.a: Standard form shows the y-intercept and makes the quadratic formula easy to apply. Vertex form shows the vertex directly. Both describe the same parabola.

how: Type x^2 - 4x + 3 or any ax² + bx + c. For adjustable coefficients try a*x^2 + b*x + c and drag the sliders.
Open Key points to see where the parabola crosses the x-axis and what the y-intercept is.
The lowest or highest point appears in Key points. Check it against the axis of symmetry formula.
Drag a through zero and watch the parabola flip from opening up to opening down.
Move c until the roots merge and then disappear, which is when b² - 4ac passes through zero.

worked.title: Vertex, roots and intercept
worked.problem: Analyze y = x^2 - 4x + 3.
steps: Vertex: x = -b/(2a) = 4/2 = 2 and y = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1, so the vertex is (2, -1).
Roots: x^2 - 4x + 3 = (x - 1)(x - 3) = 0, so x = 1 and x = 3.
y-intercept: c = 3.
worked.answer: Vertex (2, -1), roots 1 and 3, y-intercept (0, 3); opens up.

worked.title: No real roots
worked.problem: Does y = x^2 + 2x + 5 cross the x-axis?
steps: Discriminant: b^2 - 4ac = 4 - 20 = -16, which is negative.
So there are no real roots. The vertex is at x = -1, y = 1 - 2 + 5 = 4, which is above the axis and the parabola opens up.
worked.answer: No: it never touches the x-axis. Vertex (-1, 4).

pages.title: Absolute Value Graphing Calculator | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph absolute value functions and watch the vertex and V-shape move as you transform them. Free grapher with sliders and key points.
intro: The absolute value function turns every negative output into a positive one, so its graph is a V with a sharp corner called the vertex. For y = a|x - h| + k the vertex is at (h, k), the two arms rise at slopes a and -a, and the graph is symmetric about the vertical line x = h. It is the simplest everyday example of a function that is piecewise linear.

Use the grapher to see how each number reshapes the V. Changing h slides it sideways, k slides it up or down, and a controls how steep the arms are, with a negative a flipping the V upside down. Absolute value equations like |x - 1| = 2 become intersection problems: graph the V and a horizontal line, and read the two crossing points. Distances on the number line follow the same logic.
points: The vertex (h, k) is the only corner and is the minimum when a is positive.
The arms have slopes a and -a, so a larger |a| gives a narrower V.
A negative a opens the V downward and makes the vertex a maximum.
|x - c| measures the distance from x to c, which is why the graph is symmetric.

examples.l: Upside-down V with vertex (3, 5) and roots at -2 and 8
Vertex (-2, 1) sits above the axis, so there are no roots
Flat bottom between 0 and 4: the sum of two distances

faq.q: How do I find the vertex of an absolute value graph?
faq.a: Set the inside of the bars to zero to get x, then evaluate the function there. For 2|x - 1| - 4, x = 1 and y = -4.

faq.q: How do I solve |x - 1| = 2 with a graph?
faq.a: Graph y = |x - 1| and y = 2. They meet at x = -1 and x = 3, which are the two solutions.

faq.q: Why does an absolute value equation sometimes have no solution?
faq.a: If the V never reaches the target height, the lines do not intersect. For example, |x| = -3 is impossible because absolute values cannot be negative.

faq.q: How can I type the absolute value bars?
faq.a: Use abs(x) or the vertical bars, as in |x - 2|. Both draw the same V.

faq.q: What changes if I multiply by a number?
faq.a: A bigger multiplier makes both arms steeper, and a fraction makes them flatter. A negative multiplier flips the whole graph.

how: Type abs(x - 1), or include a multiplier and a shift as in 2*abs(x - 1) - 4.
Find the corner and confirm it matches the numbers inside and outside the bars.
Add a horizontal line, such as y = 4 in a second row, and read where it cuts the V.
Put a minus sign in front of abs and see the vertex turn into a maximum.
Try abs(x) + abs(x - 4) to see a flat segment instead of a sharp corner.

worked.title: Vertex and intercepts
worked.problem: Analyze y = 2|x - 1| - 4.
steps: The vertex is where the inside is 0: x = 1, y = -4, so (1, -4). It opens up because 2 > 0.
x-intercepts: 2|x - 1| = 4, so |x - 1| = 2 and x = -1 or x = 3.
y-intercept: 2|0 - 1| - 4 = -2.
worked.answer: Vertex (1, -4), x-intercepts (-1, 0) and (3, 0), y-intercept (0, -2).

worked.title: Solve an absolute value equation by graphing
worked.problem: Solve |x - 2| = 5.
steps: Graph y = |x - 2| and the horizontal line y = 5.
They meet where x - 2 = 5 or x - 2 = -5, so x = 7 or x = -3.
worked.answer: x = 7 or x = -3.

pages.title: System of Inequalities Grapher | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph a system of inequalities and see the overlapping solution region shaded. A free online tool for algebra, linear programming and SAT prep.
intro: A system of inequalities asks for the points that satisfy several conditions at once. Each inequality shades one region, and the answer is the overlap, often called the feasible region. This is the graphical heart of linear programming, where limits on time, money or materials combine into a shape and the best answer sits at a corner of that shape.

Enter each inequality in its own row and look for the area where all the shading agrees. Boundaries drawn dashed are excluded, and solid ones are included. The corner points of the overlap come from where two boundary lines intersect, so solve those pairs of equations to find exact coordinates. With the default pair, y > x + 2 and y < -2x + 5, the wedge-shaped region has its tip at (1, 3).
points: The solution set is only the overlap of every shaded region.
Corner points are the intersections of boundary lines, found by solving two equations at a time.
Solid and dashed edges still matter: a dashed corner point is not part of the solution.
An empty overlap means the system has no solution, as when two regions face away from each other.

examples.l: Add y <= -x + 5: the corner where the boundaries meet is (4, 1)
Open disk of radius 4; add y > x to keep only the upper-left half
Add y > x^2 - 2: a lens-shaped region with corners at (-2, 2) and (2, 2)

faq.q: How do I find the solution region of a system?
faq.a: Graph every inequality and find where all the shaded areas overlap. Any point inside that overlap satisfies every inequality.

faq.q: How do I get the corner points?
faq.a: Replace the inequality signs with equals signs for the two boundaries that meet at the corner, then solve that pair of equations.

faq.q: Can a system of inequalities have no solution?
faq.a: Yes. If the shaded regions never overlap, such as y > x + 3 and y < x - 1, no point satisfies both.

faq.q: What if the region is unbounded?
faq.a: Some overlaps extend forever in one direction. They have corner points but no outer edge, so a maximum may not exist even if a minimum does.

faq.q: How is this used in linear programming?
faq.a: Constraints form the region, and the objective, such as profit, is tested at each corner. The best value always occurs at a corner point.

how: Solve for y so they look like y > x + 2 and y < -2x + 5.
Each gets its own shaded color. Their overlap is visible as a darker area.
Zoom until the whole overlapping region is visible, including any corners.
Turn the two relevant boundaries into equations and solve them, or read the intersection from a plotted pair of lines.
Pick one point in the overlap and test it in every original inequality.

worked.title: Overlap of two half-planes
worked.problem: Graph y > x + 2 and y < -2x + 5. Is (0, 3) a solution?
steps: The boundaries meet where x + 2 = -2x + 5, so x = 1 and y = 3: the corner is (1, 3).
Test (0, 3): 3 > 0 + 2 is true, and 3 < 0 + 5 is true.
The solution is the wedge above the first line and below the second.
worked.answer: Yes, (0, 3) is in the solution region; the boundaries meet at (1, 3).

worked.title: A triangular region
worked.problem: Graph y >= 0, y <= 4 - x and y <= 2x. Find the region's vertices and area.
steps: y = 0 meets y = 4 - x at (4, 0). y = 0 meets y = 2x at (0, 0).
2x = 4 - x gives x = 4/3 and y = 8/3.
Area = (1/2)(base 4)(height 8/3) = 16/3.

pages.title: Inverse Function Grapher (y = x Reflection) | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph a function and its inverse together. See the reflection across y = x and check domain and range with this free online grapher.
intro: An inverse function undoes the original: if f sends 2 to 8, then its inverse sends 8 back to 2. On a graph this has a beautiful consequence. Every point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on the inverse, which means the two curves are mirror images across the line y = x. Drawing that mirror line is the fastest way to check an inverse you have computed.

Not every function has an inverse that is itself a function. A curve passing the horizontal line test, meaning no horizontal line hits it twice, is one-to-one and can be inverted. Parabolas fail unless you restrict the domain to one side of the vertex. Graph your function, graph the candidate inverse and y = x, and see whether the two reflect onto each other. Cube and cube root are a classic matching pair.
points: Points swap coordinates: (a, b) on f corresponds to (b, a) on the inverse.
The graphs of f and its inverse are reflections across the line y = x.
Only one-to-one functions pass the horizontal line test and have function inverses.
The domain of f becomes the range of the inverse, and vice versa.

examples.l: Its inverse is (x - 6)/2; graph both with y = x to see the mirror
Restricting x² to x ≥ 0 makes it invertible, with inverse sqrt(x)
Its inverse is ln(x); the pair reflect across y = x

faq.q: How do I find the inverse of a function?
faq.a: Swap x and y in the equation, then solve for y. For y = 2x + 6 you get x = 2y + 6, so y = (x - 6)/2.

faq.q: What is the horizontal line test?
faq.a: Slide a horizontal line across the graph. If it ever touches the curve twice, the function is not one-to-one and has no inverse function.

faq.q: Why does x² need a restricted domain?
faq.a: Because both 2 and -2 give 4, so the output 4 could come from two inputs. Limiting to x ≥ 0 removes the duplicate.

faq.q: What does the line y = x do here?
faq.a: It is the mirror. Folding the paper along that line makes a function and its inverse land on top of each other.

faq.q: Is the inverse the same as the reciprocal?
faq.a: No. The inverse f⁻¹(x) reverses the function, while 1/f(x) is a reciprocal. They are different things despite the similar notation.

how: Enter your function, such as x^3, in the first row.
In a second row type x, which draws y = x.
Add the formula you found, for example cbrt(x), and watch it appear as the reflection.
Pick a point on the original and check that the swapped point sits on the inverse.
Imagine horizontal lines across the original. If any meets it twice, restrict the domain before inverting.

worked.title: Inverse of a cube
worked.problem: Find the inverse of f(x) = x^3 and check it with f(2).
steps: Swap x and y and solve: x = y^3, so y = cbrt(x).
f(2) = 8 and the inverse sends 8 back to cbrt(8) = 2.
The graphs are mirror images across the line y = x.
worked.answer: f^-1(x) = cbrt(x).

worked.title: Inverse of a line
worked.problem: Find the inverse of f(x) = 2x + 3.
steps: Write x = 2y + 3 and solve for y: y = (x - 3)/2.
Check: f(1) = 5 and the inverse gives (5 - 3)/2 = 1.

pages.title: Logarithmic Graphing Calculator Online | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free logarithmic function graphing calculator. Plot transformations of log curves, compare them with exponentials and find intercepts in seconds.
intro: Most logarithm problems in algebra 2 and precalculus are about transformations of the parent graph. In y = a·log(x - h) + k, the value h moves the curve and its vertical asymptote sideways, k moves it up or down, and a stretches or flips it. Identifying those three numbers from a picture, or sketching from an equation, is the whole skill.

Plot a transformed log and trace its new features. The asymptote moves to x = h, the domain becomes x > h, and the curve's key point (1, 0) shifts to (h + 1, k). A negative a reflects the graph over a horizontal line, while a negative sign on x reflects it across the y-axis and moves the domain to the left. Use the default 2·log(x + 2) - 1 to see a stretch, a left shift and a downward shift combined.
points: The vertical asymptote of log(x - h) is the line x = h, and the domain is x > h.
The parent point (1, 0) moves to (h + 1, k) after the transformation.
A negative multiplier a reflects the curve over the horizontal line y = k.
Replacing x with -x reflects across the y-axis, so the domain becomes x < 0.

examples.l: Shifted right 3 and up 2: asymptote at x = 3, passes through (4, 2)
Flipped over the x-axis and stretched by 2, now decreasing
Reflected across the y-axis: defined only for x < 0

faq.q: How do I find the asymptote of a transformed log?
faq.a: Set the inside of the log equal to zero and solve for x. For log(x + 2) that gives x = -2, which is the vertical asymptote.

faq.q: What is the domain of log(x - 3)?
faq.a: The input must be positive, so x - 3 > 0 and x > 3. The graph exists only to the right of the asymptote.

faq.q: What does a negative coefficient do?
faq.a: It flips the graph over a horizontal line. A rising log becomes a falling one, with the same asymptote.

faq.q: How does k change the graph?
faq.a: It slides everything vertically by k units. The asymptote stays put because it is a vertical line.

faq.q: How do I write the equation from a graph?
faq.a: Read the asymptote for h, a point for k and a, then substitute one more point to check your stretch factor.

how: Type log(x) or ln(x) first and note where it crosses the x-axis.
Change to ln(x - 3) + 2 and compare with the parent. Note the new asymptote.
Put a number in front, like -2*ln(x), and see which way the curve turns.
Replace x with -x to push the graph to the left of the y-axis.
Use sliders with a*ln(x - h) + k and tune a, h and k until it matches a picture from your homework.

worked.title: Shifted logarithm
worked.problem: Analyze y = 2 log(x + 2) - 1 (log means base 10 here).
steps: The argument must be positive, so x + 2 > 0: domain x > -2 with a vertical asymptote at x = -2.
y-intercept: 2 log(2) - 1 is about 0.602 - 1 = -0.398.
x-intercept: log(x + 2) = 0.5, so x + 2 = 10^0.5 is about 3.162 and x is about 1.162.
worked.answer: Domain x > -2, asymptote x = -2, y-intercept about (0, -0.398), x-intercept about (1.162, 0).

worked.title: Solve a log equation
worked.problem: Solve log base 2 of x = 3.
steps: Rewrite in exponent form: x = 2^3 = 8.
Graph y = log(x, 2) and y = 3 and read the intersection.

pages.title: Number Line Inequality Grapher | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph inequalities on a number line with open and closed circles. A free online tool to visualize solution sets for algebra homework.
intro: A number line graph is the standard way to display the solution of a one-variable inequality such as 3x - 5 > 7. First you solve it, here to x > 4, then you mark every value that works. A circle at the endpoint is open when the endpoint is excluded and closed when it is included, and an arrow shows that the solution continues forever.

This tool draws the solution set as a line segment along the x-axis, so you can see where it begins and ends. Type a condition such as x > 4 ? 0 : NaN and the ray appears only where the statement is true. Joining two conditions with && gives an interval, and || gives two separate pieces. The tool shows the extent of the set, while you add the open or closed circles yourself, following your teacher's notation.
points: Solve the inequality first, then graph the simplified result like x > 4.
Open circle means the endpoint is excluded; closed circle means it is included.
Use and for an overlap like -2 < x ≤ 4, and or for two separate pieces.
Flip the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number.

examples.l: The solution of 3x - 5 > 7, a ray from 4 to the right
Compound inequality -2 < x ≤ 4, one connected segment
Two rays: everything left of -1 or right of 3

faq.q: How do I graph an inequality on a number line?
faq.a: Solve for x, mark the endpoint with an open or closed circle, and draw an arrow in the direction that satisfies the inequality.

faq.q: When do I use an open circle?
faq.a: For strict signs, < and >. The endpoint itself does not satisfy the inequality, so it is left open.

faq.q: What does a compound inequality look like?
faq.a: An 'and' statement like -2 < x ≤ 4 is one segment between two endpoints. An 'or' statement gives two separate rays.

faq.q: Why does the inequality sign flip?
faq.a: Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses order. For -2x > 6, dividing by -2 gives x < -3.

faq.q: How do I type 'and' and 'or'?
faq.a: Use && for and, and || for or. Combine them with a conditional, as in x < -1 || x > 3 ? 0 : NaN.

how: Isolate x on paper or in your head, for example 3x - 5 > 7 becomes x > 4.
Type x > 4 ? 0 : NaN to draw the solution along the x-axis.
Zoom in at 4 and decide whether your answer needs an open or a closed circle.
Join conditions with && or ||, then compare the segment with your written answer.
Pick a number from the drawn part and from the empty part and substitute each into the original inequality.

worked.title: One inequality
worked.problem: Solve 2x + 1 > -3 and show it on a number line.
steps: Subtract 1: 2x > -4.
Divide by 2: x > -2.
Use an open circle at -2 (not included) and shade to the right.
worked.answer: x > -2, written (-2, infinity).

worked.title: A compound inequality
steps: Subtract 1 from all three parts: -8 <= 2x < 8.
Divide by 2: -4 <= x < 4.
Closed circle at -4, open circle at 4, shade between.

pages.title: Cubic Function Grapher & Inflection Points | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph cubic functions and find roots, turning points and the inflection point. Use sliders to see how each coefficient changes the curve.
intro: A cubic function has an S-shaped graph that can wiggle once up and once down before heading off in opposite directions at the two ends. The degree of three guarantees at least one real root, and up to three. Between the wiggles sit two turning points, a local maximum and a local minimum, and in the middle of the curve is an inflection point where the bend switches from one direction to the other.

Graph a cubic to find those features by sight. The default x³ - 3x + 1 has a local maximum at (-1, 3), a local minimum at (1, -1), an inflection point at (0, 1) and three real roots. When the leading coefficient is negative, the whole picture is flipped so the left end points up. Not every cubic has turning points; x³ alone just flattens briefly at the origin before continuing.
points: A cubic has at most two turning points and exactly one inflection point.
The ends go in opposite directions: up on the right if the leading coefficient is positive.
It always crosses the x-axis at least once, with a maximum of three real roots.
A repeated root makes the curve touch the axis and turn, rather than cross.

examples.l: No turning points: only a flat inflection at the origin
Local max at (0, 0), local min at (2, -4), double root at 0
Negative leading coefficient with roots at -2, 1 and 3

faq.q: How many turning points can a cubic have?
faq.a: Up to two. Some cubics have none, like x³, because the derivative never changes sign.

faq.q: What is an inflection point?
faq.a: It is where the curve changes concavity, from bending down to bending up or the reverse. For a cubic it sits exactly halfway between the two turning points.

faq.q: How many real roots does a cubic have?
faq.a: At least one and at most three. Count the x-axis crossings on the graph, counting a touch as a double root.

faq.q: How does the leading coefficient affect the graph?
faq.a: Positive means it rises on the right and falls on the left. Negative reverses both ends.

faq.q: How can I write a cubic from its roots?
faq.a: Multiply the factors, such as (x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 3), and include a leading coefficient to set the vertical stretch.

how: Type x^3 - 3x + 1 or your own coefficients. For experiments, try a*x^3 + b*x^2 + c*x + d.
Open Key points to see the roots, y-intercept and the local maximum and minimum.
Look for the middle of the S where the bend changes direction, halfway between the two turning points.
Put a minus sign in front and compare the end behavior.
Type (x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 3) and verify the roots match where the graph meets the axis.

worked.title: Turning points
worked.problem: Find the turning points of f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1.
steps: f(-1) = -1 + 3 + 1 = 3 (local maximum) and f(1) = 1 - 3 + 1 = -1 (local minimum).
The maximum is above the axis and the minimum below it, so the graph crosses the x-axis three times.
worked.answer: Local max (-1, 3), local min (1, -1), three real roots, y-intercept (0, 1).

worked.title: Only one real root
worked.problem: How many real roots does x^3 - 8 have?
steps: Factor as a difference of cubes: (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4).
The quadratic factor has discriminant 4 - 16 = -12 < 0, so it has no real roots.
worked.answer: One real root, x = 2.

pages.title: Exponential Function Graphing Calculator | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph exponential functions like y = a·bˣ, see the horizontal asymptote and compare growth and decay curves with free online sliders.
intro: Exponential functions model things that grow or shrink by a constant percentage each step: savings, populations, cooling coffee and radioactive decay. In y = a·bˣ, the starting value a is the y-intercept, and the base b controls everything else. A base above 1 means growth, a base between 0 and 1 means decay, and the x-axis is always a horizontal asymptote that the curve never touches.

Compare bases to feel the difference. At x = 1, the curve 2ˣ has reached 2, but 3ˣ has reached 3, so larger bases climb faster and cross y = 1 at the same point (0, 1). The natural base e ≈ 2.718 is special because the slope of eˣ at any point equals its height. For decay, rewrite a base like 0.5 as 2⁻ˣ, which is the mirror image across the y-axis.
points: Every basic exponential passes through (0, 1), and a·bˣ passes through (0, a).
If b > 1 the function grows; if 0 < b < 1 it decays toward the x-axis.
The horizontal asymptote is y = 0 unless the graph is shifted up or down.
Equal-sized steps in x multiply y by the same factor b, instead of adding the same amount.

examples.l: Decay: starts at 3 and halves with every step right
Natural exponential: slope equals height at every point
Slow growth at 50% per step, passing through (0, 1)

faq.q: How do I tell growth from decay?
faq.a: Look at the base. Above 1 the curve rises as x increases. Between 0 and 1 it falls toward the x-axis.

faq.q: What is the horizontal asymptote?
faq.a: For a·bˣ it is y = 0. If you add a constant k, the asymptote moves up or down to y = k.

faq.q: Why is e special?
faq.a: Its derivative equals itself, so eˣ grows at a rate exactly equal to its current size. It appears naturally in continuous growth models.

faq.q: How do I find the base from two points?
faq.a: Divide the later y-value by the earlier one when x differs by 1. The ratio is the base. For 3 and 1.5 one step apart, the base is 0.5.

faq.q: What is the difference between linear and exponential growth?
faq.a: Linear adds a constant amount per step. Exponential multiplies by a constant factor, so it starts slow and then accelerates sharply.

how: Type 2^x. The curve rises quickly to the right and flattens toward the x-axis on the left.
Tap + and enter exp(-x) or 0.5^x to see the mirror-image decay.
Multiply by a number, such as 3*0.5^x, and check the y-intercept.
Graph 2^x, 3^x and e^x together and note which is steepest for x > 0.
Trace the curve at integer x-values to see the repeated multiplication.

worked.title: Doubling
worked.problem: For f(x) = 2^x find f(3), f(-1) and the asymptote.
steps: As x gets very negative, 2^x approaches 0 but never reaches it, so y = 0 is the horizontal asymptote. The y-intercept is (0, 1).
worked.answer: f(3) = 8, f(-1) = 0.5, asymptote y = 0.

worked.title: Exponential decay
worked.problem: A value starts at 100 and falls 10% each year: V(x) = 100(0.9)^x. Find V(5).
steps: The decay factor is 1 - 0.10 = 0.9.
To fit the graph window, plot 10(0.9)^x, which is the same curve in tens.
worked.answer: About 59.05 after 5 years.

pages.title: Polynomial Graphing Calculator | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph polynomial functions of any degree. See roots, end behavior and turning points with this free online polynomial grapher.
intro: Polynomials of any degree can be sketched from two ingredients: end behavior and roots. The leading term decides where the two ends point, and each real root decides where the curve meets the x-axis. An even degree sends both ends the same way, an odd degree sends them in opposite directions, and a polynomial of degree n can turn at most n - 1 times.

Graph a polynomial to check your sketch. The default 0.2x⁴ - 2x² + 3 is an even-degree W shape with a local maximum at (0, 3) and two local minima near x = ±2.24, where the value is -2. Roots of odd multiplicity cross the axis, while roots of even multiplicity touch it and turn back. Factored form makes the roots visible, so try typing (x - 1)²(x + 2) and compare.
points: The leading term sets the end behavior: degree even or odd, coefficient positive or negative.
A degree n polynomial has at most n real roots and at most n - 1 turning points.
A root of odd multiplicity crosses the axis; even multiplicity bounces off it.
The constant term is the y-intercept, because every other term vanishes at x = 0.

examples.l: Touches the axis at 1 (double root) and crosses at -2
Four roots at ±1 and ±2, shaped like a W
Degree 5: ends in opposite directions, with four turning points

faq.q: How do I know the end behavior of a polynomial?
faq.a: Check the term with the highest power. Even degree with a positive coefficient rises on both ends; odd degree with a positive coefficient falls left and rises right.

faq.q: How many turning points can a polynomial have?
faq.a: At most one fewer than its degree. A quartic can turn three times, but it may turn fewer.

faq.q: What does a double root look like?
faq.a: The curve touches the x-axis and bounces back without crossing, like a parabola at its vertex.

faq.q: How can I find roots by graphing?
faq.a: Read the x-axis crossings from the plot or from Key points. Then confirm each by substituting it into the polynomial.

faq.q: Why does my polynomial look flat near a root?
faq.a: A higher multiplicity, such as a triple root, flattens the curve as it passes through the axis.

how: Type it in expanded or factored form, such as 0.2*x^4 - 2*x^2 + 3 or (x - 1)^2*(x + 2).
Zoom out and compare both ends with what the leading term predicts.
Note each crossing and each touch point, and compare with the factors.
Open Key points for local maxima and minima and confirm they do not exceed n - 1.
Large coefficients may need a wider view, so zoom until all features are visible.

worked.title: End behavior and roots of a quartic
worked.problem: Analyze f(x) = 0.2x^4 - 2x^2 + 3.
steps: Even degree with a positive leading coefficient: both ends point up. f(0) = 3.
Taking square roots gives x about +-2.857 and +-1.356.
worked.answer: Four real roots, about -2.857, -1.356, 1.356 and 2.857; y-intercept (0, 3).

worked.title: Factor a cubic
worked.problem: Find the roots of x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6.
steps: Try x = 1: 1 - 2 - 5 + 6 = 0, so (x - 1) is a factor.
The roots are x = 1, 3 and -2, the three x-axis crossings.
worked.answer: Roots -2, 1 and 3.

pages.title: Vertex Form Graphing Calculator | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph y = a(x − h)² + k and watch the vertex move as you drag the sliders. A free vertex form grapher for algebra and SAT prep.
intro: Vertex form writes a parabola as y = a(x - h)² + k, which hands you the vertex (h, k) directly. That makes it the best form for sketching and for describing transformations from the parent graph y = x². The number h slides the parabola sideways, k slides it up or down, and a stretches, compresses or flips it.

The only trap is the sign of h. Because the equation contains x - h, the factor (x + 2)² moves the vertex to x = -2, not +2. Drag the sliders to see this in motion, and watch the vertex travel across the plane. If a is positive, the vertex is the lowest point; if negative, the highest. The default 0.5(x - 3)² - 2 has its vertex at (3, -2) and is wider than the parent because |a| is less than 1.
points: The vertex is (h, k), read straight from the equation with the sign of h reversed.
The axis of symmetry is the vertical line x = h.
If |a| > 1 the parabola is narrower than y = x²; if |a| < 1 it is wider.
Expanding the squared factor gives the standard form ax² + bx + c.

examples.l: Opens down, narrow, with vertex (-1, 5)
Vertex on the axis at (4, 0): a double root
Drag the sliders a, h and k to move and reshape the parabola

faq.q: What is vertex form?
faq.a: It is y = a(x - h)² + k. The point (h, k) is the vertex, and a controls the width and the direction the parabola opens.

faq.q: Why does (x + 2)² move the vertex to -2?
faq.a: Because the vertex is where the squared part equals zero, and x + 2 = 0 at x = -2.

faq.q: How do I convert standard form to vertex form?
faq.a: Complete the square, or use h = -b/(2a) and then find k by substituting h into the equation.

faq.q: What does a negative a do?
faq.a: It flips the parabola to open downward, so the vertex becomes the maximum point.

faq.q: How do I find the roots from vertex form?
faq.a: Set y to zero, isolate the squared factor, and take square roots. Or read the crossings from the graph.

how: Type a*(x - h)^2 + k, or plug in numbers like 0.5*(x - 3)^2 - 2.
Move the h slider and watch the vertex slide left and right along its horizontal line.
Move k and see the whole parabola shift vertically.
Slide a below 1 for wider, above 1 for narrower, and through 0 to flip it.

pages.title: Asymptote Graphing Calculator | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Find vertical, horizontal and slant asymptotes by graphing. A free online tool that shows holes and discontinuities for precalculus and calculus.
intro: An asymptote is a line that a curve approaches but does not settle onto, and spotting one is a core skill in precalculus. Vertical asymptotes appear where a function blows up, usually at a zero of a denominator or at the edge of a logarithm. Horizontal and slant asymptotes describe where the curve heads when x grows very large in either direction.

Graph the function and zoom out to see all three kinds. For (2x + 1)/(x - 3), the curve rushes along the vertical line x = 3 and flattens toward y = 2 on both sides. Trace the curve near the suspect line and watch the y-values grow without bound. Tangent shows vertical asymptotes repeating forever, exponentials flatten toward a horizontal line, and a fraction with a higher power on top bends toward a slanted line.
points: Vertical asymptotes come from values of x that make the function undefined but not removable.
Horizontal asymptotes describe end behavior as x moves toward positive or negative infinity.
Slant asymptotes appear when the numerator is exactly one degree higher than the denominator.
A curve may cross a horizontal or slant asymptote in the middle, but never a vertical one.

Flattens toward the horizontal asymptote y = -3 on the left
Vertical asymptotes repeat at every odd multiple of π/2

faq.q: How do I find a vertical asymptote?
faq.a: Find x-values where the denominator is zero after canceling common factors. Near those values the output grows without limit, so the graph runs up or down along a vertical line.

faq.q: How do I find a horizontal asymptote?
faq.a: Compare the degrees of numerator and denominator. If the top degree is smaller the asymptote is y = 0; if the degrees match, it is the ratio of leading coefficients.

faq.q: Can a graph cross its asymptote?
faq.a: It can cross a horizontal or slant asymptote, because those describe far-away behavior. It cannot cross a vertical asymptote since the function is undefined there.

faq.q: What is the difference between an asymptote and a hole?
faq.a: A hole is one missing point where a factor cancels. An asymptote is a line the curve chases, with outputs growing without bound.

faq.q: Do exponential functions have asymptotes?
faq.a: Yes. y = 2^x - 3 gets closer and closer to y = -3 as x decreases, so y = -3 is its horizontal asymptote.

Scroll out so you can see how the curve behaves far to the left and right.

Compare the far-left and far-right height with the value you predicted from degrees.

Intercepts: x = -0.5 and y = f(0) = 1/(-3), about -0.333.

worked.title: A slant asymptote

steps: Split the fraction: f(x) = x + 1/x.
As x gets large, 1/x approaches 0, so the graph follows the slant line y = x. The denominator is 0 at x = 0, giving a vertical asymptote.
worked.answer: Vertical asymptote x = 0 and slant asymptote y = x.

intro: Slope-intercept form, y = mx + b, is the most common way to write a line because both numbers have a meaning you can see. The slope m is how fast the line rises per step to the right, and b is the height where it crosses the y-axis. Starting at (0, b) and counting rise over run gives you the second point and a complete graph in seconds.

Use sliders to feel what m and b do. Increasing m tilts the line steeper, making it negative flips the tilt, and changing b slides the line up or down without changing its angle. A fraction slope such as 2/3 means up 2 and right 3. This form also makes it easy to build an equation from a graph: read b where the line meets the y-axis, then count to find m.
points: m is rise over run; b is the y-intercept, the value of y when x equals zero.
Changing only b gives a parallel line, because the slope stays the same.
Horizontal lines have m = 0, and vertical lines cannot be written in this form.
To write an equation from two points, find m first, then solve for b.

Starts at (0, -1), then up 2 and right 3 each step

faq.q: What do m and b stand for?
faq.a: m is the slope, which measures steepness and direction. b is the y-intercept, where the line crosses the vertical axis.

faq.q: How do I graph y = mx + b by hand?
faq.a: Plot (0, b), then use the slope as rise over run to find another point, and draw the line through both.

faq.q: How do I find the equation from two points?
faq.a: Compute m as the change in y over the change in x, then substitute one point into y = mx + b to solve for b.

faq.q: What does a negative slope mean?
faq.a: The line falls from left to right. For every step right, y decreases.

faq.q: Why can't vertical lines use this form?
faq.a: A vertical line has an undefined slope, since the run is zero. Write it as x = a constant instead.

intro: Standard form, Ax + By = C, is the format you meet in word problems with two quantities and one total. If tickets cost 2 dollars and snacks cost 3, then 2x + 3y = 6 describes every combination that sums to 6 dollars. Its biggest advantage is that the intercepts are easy to find, because setting one variable to zero turns the equation into a one-step problem.

For 2x + 3y = 6, set y = 0 to get x = 3, and set x = 0 to get y = 2. Plot those two intercepts, connect them, and the line is done. This page lets you type the standard form directly and see the line, and also lets you rewrite it as y = (6 - 2x)/3 to read the slope, here -2/3. When B is zero, the line is vertical, written like x = 3.

The slope is -A/B, which you get by rearranging into y = mx + b.
If B = 0 the line is vertical; if A = 0 it is horizontal.
Standard form usually keeps A, B and C as integers with A nonnegative.

faq.a: Find both intercepts by setting each variable to zero in turn, plot them, and draw the line through them.

faq.q: How do I convert to slope-intercept form?
faq.a: Solve for y. From 2x + 3y = 6, subtract 2x and divide by 3 to get y = -2/3 x + 2.

faq.q: What is the slope of Ax + By = C?
faq.a: It is -A/B. For 4x - 5y = 20 the slope is 4/5.

faq.q: Why use standard form at all?
faq.a: It handles vertical lines, makes integer coefficients easy, and suits problems where two amounts add up to a total.

faq.q: What if C is zero?
faq.a: Then the line passes through the origin, since x = 0 and y = 0 satisfy the equation. Both intercepts are the same point.

intro: Cosine looks like sine that has been nudged to the left by a quarter cycle, and that is exactly what it is: cos(x) = sin(x + π/2). Its signature is that it starts at its maximum, 1, when x equals zero. That makes cosine the natural choice for quantities that begin at an extreme, like the height of a Ferris wheel car at the top or the position of a spring pulled to full stretch.

Cosine is also an even function, so its graph is a mirror image across the y-axis, and cos(-x) = cos(x). It crosses the x-axis at odd multiples of π/2 and reaches its minimum at π. To model real situations, combine the standard pieces: 4cos(πx/6) + 10 has a midline of 10, an amplitude of 4 and a period of 12. Use the grapher to check where your model peaks.

Even symmetry: the left half is the mirror of the right half.
Cosine equals sine shifted left by π/2, so one formula can be converted into the other.
Squares like cos²(x) stay between 0 and 1 and repeat every π.

faq.q: Where does the cosine graph start?

faq.q: Is cosine really just a shifted sine?
faq.a: Yes. Shifting sine left by π/2 gives cosine, so either can describe the same wave with a different phase.

faq.q: Why is cosine an even function?
faq.a: Because cos(-x) = cos(x). The graph is symmetric about the y-axis, like a parabola.

faq.q: Where are the zeros of cosine?
faq.a: At x = π/2, 3π/2 and every odd multiple of π/2, where the curve crosses the axis.

faq.q: How do I model a cycle that starts at a peak?
faq.a: Use a cosine with no phase shift, such as A cos(Bx) + D. A sine model would need an extra shift to start at the top.

intro: The sine wave is the shape of everything that oscillates: sound, alternating current, tides, a swinging pendulum. In y = A sin(B(x - C)) + D, each letter is a physical property of the wave. A is the amplitude, the distance from the midline to a peak. B sets the frequency, so the period is 2π/B. C is the phase shift, and D moves the midline up or down.

Plot one wave, then change a single number at a time. Doubling B squeezes the wave into half the width, and halving it stretches the wave to twice the length. Frequency is the number of cycles per unit, the reciprocal of the period.

faq.q: How do I find the amplitude of a sine wave?
faq.a: Take half the difference between the maximum and the minimum. For 3 sin(2x) the peaks are 3 and -3, so the amplitude is 3.

faq.q: How do I find the period?
faq.a: Divide 2π by the number multiplying x. For sin(2x) the period is 2π/2 = π, so the wave repeats every π units.

faq.q: What is phase shift?
faq.a: It is a horizontal slide of the whole wave. In sin(x - π/2) the wave moves right by π/2.

faq.q: What is the difference between frequency and period?
faq.a: Period is the length of one cycle, and frequency is how many cycles fit in one unit. They are reciprocals of each other.

faq.q: Why does adding two sine waves look irregular?
faq.a: The waves reinforce each other where they peak together and cancel where they oppose, so the sum no longer repeats as a simple cycle.

pages.desc: Graph the unit circle x² + y² = 1 and explore sine and cosine ratios at any angle in degrees or radians with this free interactive tool.
intro: The unit circle is a circle of radius 1 centered at the origin, and it is the reason sine and cosine exist as functions of any angle. A point on the circle at angle θ has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ), so the x-coordinate is the cosine and the y-coordinate is the sine. Everything you memorize about special angles comes from reading points on this single picture.

faq.q: What is the unit circle?
faq.a: A circle with radius 1 centered at the origin. Its equation is x² + y² = 1.

faq.q: How do I read sine and cosine from it?
faq.a: For an angle θ measured from the positive x-axis, the point's x-coordinate is cos θ and its y-coordinate is sin θ.

faq.q: Why are the special angles important?
faq.a: Angles like 30°, 45° and 60° have exact values that show up everywhere in trig. The unit circle lets you recover them rather than memorize them.

faq.q: How do radians relate to the circle?
faq.a: One radian is the angle whose arc length equals the radius. Since the circumference is 2π, a full turn is 2π radians.

faq.q: How can I check my values?

intro: Conic sections are the four curves you get by slicing a cone: the circle, the ellipse, the parabola and the hyperbola. They look unrelated but they all come from one general equation, Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0, and the coefficients decide which curve you get. Learning to identify the type from the equation is the first step in any conics unit.

Use this page as a hub to compare all four. A circle and an ellipse have x² and y² with the same sign, and they are equal for a circle. A hyperbola has opposite signs on the squared terms. A parabola has only one squared term. The discriminant B² - 4AC summarizes the test: negative gives an ellipse or circle, zero a parabola and positive a hyperbola.

A parabola has just one squared variable, such as y² = 4x or y = x².
The discriminant B² - 4AC separates the cases: negative, zero or positive.
A term with xy means the conic is rotated away from the axes.

faq.q: What are the four conic sections?

faq.q: How do I tell conics apart from the equation?
faq.a: Look at the squared terms. Same sign and equal coefficients give a circle, same sign and different coefficients give an ellipse, opposite signs a hyperbola, and one squared term a parabola.

faq.q: What is the discriminant of a conic?
faq.a: For Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + ..., it is B² - 4AC. Negative means an ellipse, zero a parabola and positive a hyperbola.

faq.q: Why do some conics fail the vertical line test?
faq.a: Circles, ellipses and sideways parabolas double back over the same x-values, so they are not functions. They are graphed as implicit curves.

faq.q: What does the xy term do?
faq.a: It rotates the curve. Without it, the axes of the conic line up with the coordinate axes.
