pages.title: Circle Equation Grapher (Center & Radius) | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph a circle from its equation and read the center and radius instantly. A free online circle grapher for geometry and algebra practice.
intro: The standard equation of a circle, (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², tells you everything at once. The center is (h, k) and the radius is r. Setting both h and k to zero gives x² + y² = r², the circle centered at the origin. The key skill is reading h and k with the right signs: (x + 3)² means the center's x-coordinate is -3.

Equations often arrive in expanded form, like x² + y² - 6x + 8y = 0, and you need to complete the square to find the center and radius. Here the result is (x - 3)² + (y + 4)² = 25, so the center is (3, -4) with radius 5. Graph both forms and confirm they match. A circle is not a function of x because each x gives two y-values, so it is plotted as an implicit curve.
points: In (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², the center is (h, k) and the radius is r.
The right-hand side is r², so take its square root to get the radius.
Completing the square converts the expanded form into center-radius form.
A strict inequality such as x² + y² < 9 shades the interior of the circle.

examples.l: Center (3, -2), radius 5
Complete the square: center (3, -4), radius 5, passing through the origin
Open disk of radius 3: the interior, with a dashed edge

faq.q: How do I find the center and radius from an equation?
faq.a: Rewrite it as (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r². The center is (h, k), and the radius is the square root of the right side.

faq.q: Why does (x + 3)² mean the center is at -3?
faq.a: Because x + 3 equals zero at x = -3. The sign in the equation is opposite to the coordinate.

faq.q: How do I complete the square for a circle?
faq.a: Group the x terms and the y terms, add the square of half the coefficient to both sides for each, and factor into perfect squares.

faq.q: What happens if the right side is zero or negative?
faq.a: A right side of zero gives a single point, and a negative right side gives no real graph at all.

faq.q: Is a circle a function?
faq.a: No. Most x-values give two y-values, one on the top half and one on the bottom half, so it fails the vertical line test.

how: Enter (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25 and the circle is drawn at once.
Find the midpoint of the circle and compare with (h, k) from the equation.
Count from the center to the edge and compare it with the square root of the right side.
Enter an expanded equation and the standard form, then check that the two circles coincide.
Replace = with < to fill the disk.

worked.title: Complete the square
worked.problem: Find the center and radius of x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0.
steps: Group terms: (x^2 - 6x) + (y^2 + 4y) = 12.
Complete the squares by adding 9 and 4 to both sides: (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25.
Center (3, -2), radius sqrt(25) = 5.
worked.answer: Center (3, -2), radius 5.

worked.title: Write an equation
worked.problem: Write the circle with center (-1, 2) and radius 3, and test (2, 2).
steps: At (2, 2): (3)^2 + 0 = 9, so the point is on the circle.

pages.title: Ellipse Graphing Calculator | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph horizontal and vertical ellipses from their standard-form equation. See the center and axes change with sliders in this free grapher.
intro: An ellipse is a stretched circle. In x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, the numbers a and b are the half-lengths along the x and y directions. The larger one sets the major axis, the longer way across, and the smaller one sets the minor axis. A circle is the special case where a equals b.

Every ellipse hides two special points called foci, placed on the major axis at distance c from the center, where c² = a² - b² when a is the larger. For x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, a = 5, b = 3 and c = 4, so the foci are at (±4, 0). Eccentricity, c/a, measures how stretched the ellipse is: 0 for a circle and close to 1 for a long thin one. Planets move on ellipses with the sun at one focus.
points: The vertices are at distance a from the center along the major axis.
The foci are at distance c from the center, where c² = a² - b².
Whichever denominator is larger tells you the direction of the major axis.
Eccentricity c/a measures how far the ellipse is from being a circle.

examples.l: Taller than wide: the major axis is vertical and the foci are at (0, ±4)
Shifted ellipse: center (2, -1), a = 4 and b = 2
Equal denominators: a circle of radius 2

faq.q: How do I find a and b?
faq.a: Take the square roots of the denominators. For x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 that gives a = 5 and b = 3.

faq.q: How do I know if the major axis is horizontal or vertical?
faq.a: Whichever variable has the larger denominator. If x² has the larger one, the ellipse is wider than tall.

faq.q: What are the foci of an ellipse?
faq.a: Two fixed points on the major axis. The sum of the distances from any point on the curve to the two foci is constant.

faq.q: How do I find the foci?
faq.a: Compute c = √(a² - b²) and measure c units from the center along the major axis.

faq.q: What is eccentricity?
faq.a: It is c divided by a. A value near 0 means almost a circle, and a value near 1 means a long, flat shape.

how: Type x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1 for a wide ellipse centered at the origin.
Read the vertices on each axis and compare them with a and b.
Compute c from a and b and mark the points on the major axis.
Swap the denominators and see the major axis turn vertical.
Add (x - 2) and (y + 1) inside the squares to move the ellipse to a new center.

worked.title: Foci of a horizontal ellipse
worked.problem: Find the vertices and foci of x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1.
steps: a^2 = 25 and b^2 = 9, so a = 5 (the larger one, under x^2) and b = 3.
Vertices (+-5, 0), co-vertices (0, +-3).
c^2 = a^2 - b^2 = 16, so c = 4 and the foci are (+-4, 0).
worked.answer: Vertices (+-5, 0), foci (+-4, 0).

worked.title: A vertical ellipse
worked.problem: Find the foci of 9x^2 + 4y^2 = 36.
steps: Divide by 36: x^2/4 + y^2/9 = 1. The larger denominator 9 is under y^2, so the major axis is vertical with a = 3 and b = 2.

pages.title: Hyperbola Graphing Calculator | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph a hyperbola from its equation and see both branches and the asymptotes. A free online grapher for precalculus and conics review.
intro: A hyperbola has two separate branches that open away from each other, each bending toward a pair of crossing lines called asymptotes. In x²/a² - y²/b² = 1 the branches open left and right, with vertices at (±a, 0). If the minus sign comes before x² instead, the branches open up and down. The minus sign between the squared terms is the giveaway that you are looking at a hyperbola.

The asymptotes of x²/4 - y²/9 = 1 are y = ±(3/2)x, found by replacing the 1 with a 0 and solving. The foci lie on the same axis as the vertices, at distance c from the center where c² = a² + b², which differs from the ellipse rule by a sign. Here c = √13, about 3.6. The curve never touches its asymptotes, but gets closer the farther out you go.
points: The positive squared term tells you which way the branches open.
Asymptotes come from setting the right side to zero: y = ±(b/a)x for the horizontal case.
The foci satisfy c² = a² + b², further from the center than the vertices.
A rectangular hyperbola has a = b, so its asymptotes are perpendicular.

examples.l: Opens up and down, with vertices at (0, ±3)
Shifted: center (1, -2), vertices at (-2, -2) and (4, -2)
Rectangular hyperbola with perpendicular asymptotes y = ±x

faq.q: How do I tell which way a hyperbola opens?
faq.a: Look for the positive squared term. If x² is positive the branches open left and right; if y² is positive they open up and down.

faq.q: How do I find the asymptotes?
faq.a: Set the right-hand side to zero and solve for y. For x²/4 - y²/9 = 0, y = ±(3/2)x.

faq.q: How do I find the foci?
faq.a: Use c² = a² + b². For a = 2 and b = 3, c = √13 ≈ 3.61, so the foci are at (±3.61, 0).

faq.q: How is a hyperbola different from an ellipse?
faq.a: An ellipse has a plus sign and is a closed loop. A hyperbola has a minus sign and has two open branches.

faq.q: What is a rectangular hyperbola?
faq.a: One with a = b. Its asymptotes meet at right angles. The graph of xy = 1 is the same curve, rotated 45 degrees.

how: Type x^2/4 - y^2/9 = 1 and look at the two branches.
Read where each branch crosses the axis and compare with ±a.
Add y = 1.5x and y = -1.5x as lines and see how the branches follow them.
Put the minus sign in front of x² instead to rotate the branches to up and down.
Replace x and y with (x - 1) and (y + 2) to move the hyperbola to a new center.

worked.title: Asymptotes and foci
worked.problem: Analyze x^2/4 - y^2/9 = 1.
steps: The x^2 term is positive, so the branches open left and right with a = 2 and b = 3. Vertices (+-2, 0).
Asymptotes: y = +-(b/a)x = +-1.5x.
c^2 = a^2 + b^2 = 13, so the foci are (+-sqrt(13), 0), about (+-3.606, 0).
worked.answer: Vertices (+-2, 0), asymptotes y = +-1.5x, foci about (+-3.606, 0).

worked.title: A vertical hyperbola
worked.problem: Analyze y^2/9 - x^2/16 = 1.
steps: The y^2 term is positive, so the branches open up and down: a = 3, b = 4. Vertices (0, +-3).
Asymptotes: y = +-(a/b)x = +-0.75x.
c^2 = 9 + 16 = 25, so the foci are (0, +-5).
worked.answer: Vertices (0, +-3), asymptotes y = +-0.75x, foci (0, +-5).

pages.title: 3D Graphing Calculator: z = f(x, y) Surfaces | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Plot 3D surfaces z = f(x, y) and implicit equations like x² + y² + z² = 9 online. Rotate, zoom and read a colour legend, free in your browser.
intro: This 3D graphing calculator plots a surface z = f(x, y). Type a formula in x and y, then drag to rotate the surface, scroll or pinch to zoom, and use the range boxes to choose which part of the surface to see. Letters other than x and y, such as a or b, become sliders so you can watch how a parameter changes the shape. It also draws implicit surfaces such as the sphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9 when you type an equation that contains z.

ul: Type the right-hand side only, for example x^2 + y^2. Starting with z = is also fine.
For a closed or implicit surface, type an equation in x, y and z, such as x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9. The plotter finds every point where both sides are equal.
Use * for multiplication or write sin(x)cos(y). Use ^ for powers and sqrt(), abs() or |x| for roots and absolute value.
Functions include sin, cos, tan, exp, ln, log, sqrt and abs. Angles are in radians.
Any other single letter, such as a or b, becomes a slider from −5 to 5.
Drag (or use the arrow keys) to rotate, scroll or pinch to zoom, and double-click to reset the view.
Top view looks straight down on the surface with no perspective, so the colours read like a contour map of height.
Detail sets the grid resolution. Use Fine for smooth curves and Fast on slower phones. Implicit surfaces use a 3D grid, so Fast is a good choice for the busiest ones.
For an implicit surface, z min and z max set the height of the box (default −6 to 6). Widen the ranges if part of the surface is cut off.
Set z min and z max to clip tall spikes so you can see the interesting part of surfaces such as 1/(x^2 + y^2).
Paraboloid: z = x^2 + y^2, a bowl that opens upward.
Saddle: z = x^2 − y^2, which curves up along one axis and down along the other.
Ripple: z = sin(sqrt(x^2 + y^2)), circular waves around the origin.
Gaussian: z = exp(−(x^2 + y^2)/4), a smooth hill.
Cone: z = sqrt(x^2 + y^2).
Monkey saddle: z = x^3 − 3xy^2, which has room for three downward slopes.
Sphere: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9.
Torus: (sqrt(x^2 + y^2) − 3)^2 + z^2 = 1, a doughnut.
Hyperboloid: x^2 + y^2 − z^2 = 1, an hourglass that opens up and down.
Gyroid: sin(x)cos(y) + sin(y)cos(z) + sin(z)cos(x) = 0, a repeating sponge-like sheet.

p: The colour shows height: dark purple is the lowest point in view and yellow is the highest, and the colour bar at the right lists the values. The numbers on the box edges show the x and y ranges. Because the height axis is scaled to fit the box, compare heights using the numbers rather than the visual size alone.

faq.q: Can it plot a sphere or other implicit surfaces such as x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9?
faq.a: Yes. Type the equation with z on either side, for example x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9. The plotter samples the box and extracts the surface with a method called marching tetrahedra. Inequalities such as x^2 + y^2 + z^2 < 9 are not supported.

faq.q: Why are parts of my surface missing?
faq.a: Points where the formula has no real value, such as the square root of a negative number or division by zero, are left blank. Points outside your z min and z max limits are also left blank.

faq.q: Why is my surface a flat sheet or very spiky?
faq.a: A very tall spike makes the rest of the surface look flat because the height is scaled to fit. Set z min and z max, or narrow the x and y ranges, to zoom into the part you care about.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Drag with one finger to rotate and pinch with two fingers to zoom. If the surface is slow to draw, choose Fast detail.

faq.q: Are angles in degrees or radians?
faq.a: Radians, so sin(x) uses x in radians, as in most calculus courses.

faq.q: Can I save the picture?
faq.a: Use Save PNG to download the current view as an image.

pages.title: Parametric Equation Grapher & Lissajous Plots | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph parametric equations x(t), y(t) and Lissajous curves online. A free parametric grapher with sliders to explore circles, spirals and loops.
intro: A parametric curve describes x and y separately in terms of a third variable, usually t, written as the pair (x(t), y(t)). Instead of asking what y is for a given x, you ask where a moving point is at time t. That makes parametric form the natural choice for circles, ellipses, loops and any path that crosses itself, none of which can be written as a single y = f(x).

In calculus the topic matters because it extends slope and arc length to curves such as projectile paths and cycloids. The slope at a point is dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), and the curve has a vertical tangent wherever dx/dt = 0 while dy/dt is not. Type a pair in parentheses with t as the variable, and the grapher traces the path for you. The default (cos(t), sin(t)) is the unit circle, and doubling the first component stretches it into an ellipse.
points: Write the pair as (x(t), y(t)) with the variable t, for example (cos(t), sin(t)).
Changing the coefficient on one component stretches the curve in that direction only.
Different frequencies inside sine and cosine produce Lissajous figures with loops and crossings.
The path is drawn for t from 0 up to a few turns, so curves that need a longer range may look cut off.

examples.l: Ellipse: semi-axes 2 and 1
Lissajous curve with 3 horizontal and 2 vertical oscillations
Cycloid: the path of a point on a rolling wheel
Drag a to change the circle radius

faq.q: What does the t in a parametric equation mean?
faq.a: It is a helper variable, often thought of as time. Each value of t gives one point (x(t), y(t)), and the curve is the path of all those points as t changes.

faq.q: How do I find the slope of a parametric curve?
faq.a: Divide the rates of change: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). For (cos(t), sin(t)) that gives -cos(t)/sin(t), which is -cot(t). Graph the curve to check the sign of the slope on each part of the path.

faq.q: How do I turn a parametric equation into y = f(x)?
faq.a: Solve one equation for t and substitute it into the other. For (t, t^2) you get y = x^2. For a circle you eliminate t with cos(t)^2 + sin(t)^2 = 1 and get x^2 + y^2 = 1, which you can also graph directly.

faq.q: Why does my curve look cut off?
faq.a: The path is drawn over a fixed range of t. If your curve needs a larger range, rescale t inside the formula, for example use (t/3 - sin(t/3), 1 - cos(t/3)), which stretches the same shape over a longer stretch of t.

faq.q: Can I use degrees instead of radians?
faq.a: Yes. Tap the RAD or DEG chip next to the equations. In degree mode the trig functions in the pair use degrees, which is convenient for angle-based problems.

worked.title: Eliminate the parameter
worked.problem: Describe the curve x = 2cos t, y = sin t.
steps: Solve for the trig functions: cos t = x/2 and sin t = y.
Use cos²t + sin²t = 1: (x/2)² + y² = 1, which is x²/4 + y² = 1.
That is an ellipse centered at the origin with semi-axes 2 (horizontal) and 1 (vertical).
Check two values of t: t = 0 gives (2, 0) and t = π/2 gives (0, 1), both on the ellipse.
worked.answer: An ellipse, x²/4 + y² = 1, traced once counterclockwise as t goes from 0 to 2π.

worked.title: One arch of a cycloid
worked.problem: For x = t − sin t, y = 1 − cos t, find the points at t = 0, π and 2π.
steps: t = π: x = π − 0 ≈ 3.142 and y = 1 − (−1) = 2, so the top of the arch is (π, 2).
t = 2π: x = 2π − 0 ≈ 6.283 and y = 1 − 1 = 0, so the curve is back on the x-axis.
worked.answer: One arch has width 2π ≈ 6.283 and height 2. The path of a point on a rolling wheel repeats this arch.

pages.title: Polar Graphing Calculator (Roses & Cardioids) | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph polar equations such as roses, cardioids and spirals in your browser. A free polar graphing calculator with degree and radian modes.
intro: Polar coordinates locate a point by its distance r from the origin and its angle t from the positive x-axis. A polar equation such as r = 2*sin(3*t) gives the distance for every angle, so a simple formula can describe shapes that are awkward in rectangular form: roses, spirals, cardioids and limacons.

Polar graphs show up in AP Calculus BC and in precalculus, where you convert between systems with x = r cos t and y = r sin t, find area enclosed by a curve, and count petals. Type your equation as r = f(t) and the grapher plots it. The default pair shows a three-petal rose, r = 2 sin 3t, next to a cardioid, r = 1 + cos t, so you can compare how the coefficient and the added constant change the shape.
points: Write the equation as r = f(t); the letter t stands for the angle.
For r = a sin(nt) or a cos(nt), the number of petals is n when n is odd and 2n when n is even.
In r = a + b cos t, the ratio a/b decides whether the curve has a dimple, a cusp or an inner loop.
Switch between radians and degrees with the angle chip before you type angle values.

examples.l: Four-petal rose (n = 2 is even, so 2n petals)
Limacon with an inner loop
A circle of diameter 3 sitting on the x-axis
Drag a to see the rose grow without changing its petal count

faq.q: How do I convert polar to rectangular coordinates?
faq.a: Use x = r cos t, y = r sin t, and r^2 = x^2 + y^2. For example r = 3 becomes x^2 + y^2 = 9. You can graph both forms here and see that they give the same circle.

faq.q: How many petals will my rose curve have?
faq.a: For r = a sin(nt) or r = a cos(nt) with a whole number n, odd n gives n petals and even n gives 2n petals. Try n = 2, 3, 4 and 5 and count them.

faq.q: What is the difference between a cardioid and a limacon?
faq.a: A cardioid is r = a + a cos t, where the constant equals the coefficient, so it has a single cusp. When the constant is smaller than the coefficient the limacon gets an inner loop, and when it is larger the curve is a smooth or dimpled shape.

faq.q: Can r be negative?
faq.a: Yes. A negative r plots the point in the opposite direction from the angle, and the graph handles this automatically.

faq.q: Can I find the area inside a polar curve here?
faq.a: This page draws the curve; it does not compute the integral. For area use A = (1/2) times the integral of r^2 dt over the angle range, then use the picture to choose the limits.

worked.title: Petals of a rose curve
worked.problem: Sketch r = 2cos(2t): how many petals does it have and where are the tips?
steps: For r = a·cos(nt) with n even there are 2n petals, so n = 2 gives 4 petals.
The tips are where |r| = 2: t = 0 gives r = 2, so the point (2, 0). At t = π/2, r = 2cos π = −2, a negative r, so the point is plotted opposite the angle, at (0, −2).
By symmetry the other tips are (−2, 0) and (0, 2).
worked.answer: A four-petal rose with tips at (2, 0), (0, 2), (−2, 0) and (0, −2).

worked.title: Convert a polar equation to rectangular form
worked.problem: Write r = 3 sin t in x and y and identify the graph.
steps: Use x = r cos t, y = r sin t and r² = x² + y².
Multiply both sides by r: r² = 3r sin t, so x² + y² = 3y.
Complete the square: x² + (y − 1.5)² = 2.25.
worked.answer: A circle with center (0, 1.5) and radius 1.5, which sits on top of the origin.

pages.title: Derivative Graphing Calculator f'(x) | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph a function and its derivative with d/dx( ). See slopes, maxima and minima line up, then check the second derivative too. Free online.
intro: The derivative of a function is its slope at every point, and drawing f and f' on the same axes makes that relationship easy to see. Wherever f' is positive, the original function is rising. Wherever f' is negative, f is falling. And every place f' crosses the x-axis is a spot where f flattens out, which is where local maxima and minima live.

Wrap any function in d/dx( ) and the grapher draws its derivative, finds the exact formula and lists the rules it used in the Formula & steps panel, so you can check your own working. The default graph pairs f(x) = x^3 - 3x with d/dx(x^3 - 3*x), which gives 3*x^2 - 3. The derivative crosses zero at x = -1 and x = 1, exactly where f has a peak and a valley, and the Key points panel lists those turning points. Use d2/dx2( ) for the second derivative. The formula is exact but not always fully simplified, and where the slopes from the left and right disagree, such as |x| at 0, the derivative is undefined and the graph leaves a gap.
points: Type d/dx(f) to graph the derivative of f; type d2/dx2(f) for the second derivative.
The Formula & steps panel shows the exact derivative and each rule used: power, product, quotient and chain rule.
Where the derivative is above the x-axis, f is increasing; where it is below, f is decreasing.
The roots of the derivative line up with the maxima and minima of f, and they appear under Key points.
At a corner or jump, such as |x| at 0, the derivative is undefined and the curve has a gap.
Letters become sliders, so d/dx(a*x^2) lets you drag a and watch the slope function change.

examples.l: Product rule: see both the formula and the steps in the panel
Chain rule: the answer is 2*x*cos(x^2)
Matches 1/x: large near 0 and fading as x grows
Second derivative 6*x: zero at the inflection point x = 0
Jumps from -1 to 1 and is undefined at the corner x = 0
Slider a: the slope function is the line 2*a*x

faq.q: Does this calculator show the derivative formula and steps?
faq.a: Yes. Type d/dx( ) around a function. The curve is drawn from the exact derivative, and the Formula & steps panel shows the formula and the rules used, in the same syntax as the equation boxes, so you can copy it. It handles polynomials, powers, roots, quotients, exponentials, logs, trig, inverse trig and hyperbolic functions, including chains and products. Formulas are not always fully simplified.

faq.q: How can I tell where a function has a maximum or minimum?
faq.a: Graph f and d/dx(f). Where the derivative crosses the x-axis and changes sign, f has a turning point: positive to negative is a local maximum, negative to positive is a local minimum. Key points marks the roots of the derivative.

faq.q: What does it mean if the derivative is zero but f has no peak?
faq.a: Then the function only flattens out for a moment, like x^3 at x = 0. The derivative touches zero but does not change sign, so the point is a flat inflection, not an extremum.

faq.q: How do I see the second derivative?
faq.a: Type d2/dx2(f), or nest it as d/dx(d/dx(f)). Where it is positive the graph of f is concave up, where it is negative f is concave down, and a sign change marks an inflection point.

faq.q: What if the function has no exact formula?
faq.a: For functions the rules do not cover, such as floor(x) or a piecewise function written with ?:, the curve is computed numerically and the panel says so. The values are accurate for smooth functions, and corners and jumps still show as gaps.

worked.title: Maximum and minimum from the derivative
worked.problem: For f(x) = x³ − 3x, find the local extrema and say which is which.
steps: Second derivative: f″(x) = 6x. At x = −1, f″ = −6 < 0, so a local maximum. At x = 1, f″ = 6 > 0, so a local minimum.
On the graph, f′ crosses the x-axis exactly where f turns around.
worked.answer: Local maximum (−1, 2) and local minimum (1, −2).

worked.title: Product rule at a point
worked.problem: Find the derivative of x² sin x and evaluate it at x = π.
steps: Product rule: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ with u = x² and v = sin x.
d/dx(x² sin x) = 2x sin x + x² cos x.
worked.answer: The derivative is 2x sin x + x² cos x, and at x = π it equals −π² ≈ −9.87. Graph d/dx(x^2*sin(x)) and read the value at x = π.

pages.title: Integral Calculator: Area Under a Curve | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Shade the area under a curve with int(f, a, b) and see the value. Also graph the accumulation function. Free online integral grapher for calculus.
intro: Integration reverses differentiation, and graphing both a function and its antiderivative shows how the two ideas connect. If F is an antiderivative of f, then the change in F between two x-values equals the area under f between them. That statement is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and you can see it with your own eyes by comparing the heights of the two curves.

Two forms do the work. int(f, a, b) draws f, shades the signed area between a and b and prints its value on the graph, so int(x^2, 0, 3) shows 9. The Formula & steps panel then gives an antiderivative F and the step F(b) - F(a) = 9 - 0 = 9. int(f) draws the accumulation function, the area from 0 to x, so int(x^2) is the curve x^3/3, and int(f, a) starts the area at a instead of 0. Put a letter in a bound, as in int(x^2, 0, b), and drag the slider to watch the area grow. Exact antiderivatives cover polynomials, sums, constant multiples and standard functions of a linear part, such as sin(2x + 1) or 1/(3x - 1). Other integrals, such as x*sin(x), show only the numerical value from Simpson's rule, which is accurate for smooth functions.
points: int(f, a, b) shades the area between the curve and the x-axis and shows the value; area below the axis counts as negative.
The Formula & steps panel shows an antiderivative F and F(b) - F(a) when the integrand is a standard form.
int(f) is the accumulation function F(x), the area from 0 to x, so its slope equals f.
Put a letter in a bound, such as int(x^2, 0, b), to get a slider for the upper limit.
To check an antiderivative, graph int(f) and your F: they should differ by a constant, which is the C.
In US Exam Mode the printed value and the steps are hidden, like the other hints.

examples.l: Area under one arch of sine: exactly 2
Area under 1/x from 1 to e: exactly 1
Signed area: the part below the axis counts as negative
Slider b: the area grows like b^3/3
Accumulation function of cosine: it traces sin(x)

faq.q: Can this calculator shade the area under a curve?
faq.a: Yes. Type int(f, a, b), for example int(x^2, 0, 3). It shades the region between the curve and the x-axis from a to b and prints the value, which is the signed area.

faq.q: Which integrals get an exact formula?
faq.a: Polynomials, sums and differences, constant multiples, powers of a linear expression, 1/(linear), and e^x, sin, cos, tan, sinh, cosh, ln and sqrt of a linear expression. Products such as x*sin(x) and most quotients need techniques like integration by parts, so they show only the numerical value.

faq.q: Why does the constant C not matter for a definite integral?
faq.a: Because F(b) - F(a) subtracts it away. Graph int(x^2) and x^3/3 + c with a slider for c: the curves are vertical shifts of each other, so the difference in height between two x-values never changes.

faq.q: What does negative area mean?
faq.a: A definite integral counts area below the x-axis as negative. The shading shows both parts, and the printed value is the signed total, which is why int(sin(x), 0, 2*pi) is 0.

faq.q: How do I check an antiderivative?
faq.a: Graph int(f) and your own F. If your F is right the two curves are the same shape and differ only by a vertical shift. You can also graph d/dx(F) and compare it with f.

worked.title: The Fundamental Theorem on a familiar curve
worked.problem: Evaluate the integral of sin x from 0 to π.
steps: An antiderivative of sin x is −cos x.
Apply F(b) − F(a) with F(x) = −cos x: F(π) = −cos π = 1 and F(0) = −cos 0 = −1.
The graph shows one hump of the sine curve above the axis, and its area is 2.
worked.answer: The value is 2.

worked.title: Net area versus total area
worked.problem: Evaluate the integral of x² − 2 from −1 to 2 and explain the sign.
steps: An antiderivative is F(x) = x³/3 − 2x.
The negative result means more of the area is below the x-axis than above it: the curve is below the axis until x = √2 ≈ 1.414.
worked.answer: The net signed area is −3. The total unsigned area is larger, about 4.10, because the region above the axis (about 0.55) does not cancel the part below (about 3.55) but is added to it.

pages.title: Tangent Line Graphing Calculator | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph a curve together with its tangent line at any point. A free online tangent line grapher to see slope and linear approximation clearly.
intro: A tangent line touches a curve at one point and has the same slope as the curve there. Finding it is one of the first applications of the derivative: compute f'(a) to get the slope, then use the point-slope form y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a). Seeing the line sit just on the curve makes the idea of a local linear approximation much more concrete.

Graph the function and the tangent line together to check your work. The default pair is f(x) = x^2 and y = 4x - 4. At x = 2 the function equals 4 and the slope is 2 times 2 = 4, so the tangent is y - 4 = 4(x - 2), which simplifies to 4x - 4. To explore how the tangent changes as you slide along the curve, use the slider example below, where the tangent to x^2 at any x = a is y = 2ax - a^2, and drag a.
points: The slope of the tangent at x = a is f'(a), and the line passes through (a, f(a)).
Use y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a); the slope and the point are the only two ingredients.
Near the touching point, the tangent line is a good approximation of the function.
A vertical tangent has no slope, and a corner such as |x| at 0 has no tangent at all.

examples.l: Tangent at x = 1 is y = 3x - 2: add that line to check
Tangent line to x^2 at x = a; drag the slider a (add x^2 for the curve)
Tangent at x = 0 is y = x: add it and zoom in near the origin
Tangent at x = 4 is y = x/4 + 1; zoom in to see them merge
The slope function 3x^2: its value at x = 1 is the tangent slope 3

faq.q: How do I write the equation of a tangent line?
faq.a: Find f(a) and f'(a), then write y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a). For f(x) = x^2 at a = 2, that is y = 4 + 4(x - 2) = 4x - 4.

faq.q: What is a normal line?
faq.a: A normal line is perpendicular to the tangent at the same point, so its slope is the negative reciprocal, -1/f'(a). Graph it as another equation to see the right angle.

faq.q: Why does the tangent cross the curve sometimes?
faq.a: A tangent only matches the curve locally. For x^3 at 0 the tangent y = 0 passes through the curve because the graph changes concavity there.

faq.q: What is linear approximation?
faq.a: It is using the tangent line to estimate the function near a, since f(x) is approximately f(a) + f'(a)(x - a). The closer x is to a, the better the estimate; zoom in to watch the two curves merge.

faq.q: Does the grapher find the tangent automatically?
faq.a: Not the line itself. You can graph the slope function with d/dx( ) to read the slope at your point, then write the tangent from y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) and graph it to confirm that it touches the curve once without cutting through it.

worked.title: Tangent line to a parabola
worked.problem: Find the tangent line to f(x) = x² at x = 2.
steps: The point is (2, f(2)) = (2, 4).
The slope is f′(2) = 2·2 = 4.
Point-slope form: y − 4 = 4(x − 2), so y = 4x − 4.
worked.answer: y = 4x − 4. On the graph the line touches the parabola at (2, 4) and stays below it everywhere else.

worked.title: Linear approximation of a square root
worked.problem: Use the tangent line to f(x) = √x at x = 4 to estimate √4.2.
steps: The tangent line is y = 2 + (1/4)(x − 4) = x/4 + 1.
worked.answer: √4.2 ≈ 2.05. The true value is 2.0494, so the tangent line is off by less than 0.001 this close to x = 4.

pages.title: Slope Field & Solution Curve Grapher | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Draw a slope field for dy/dx = f(x, y) and a solution curve through any starting point. Free online slope field grapher for AP Calculus BC.
intro: A slope field is a picture of a differential equation. At each point (x, y) a short segment shows the slope dy/dx that the equation prescribes, and a solution curve is any curve that follows those segments. Slope fields appear in AP Calculus BC and in college differential equations because they let you describe solutions without solving the equation.

Type dy/dx = followed by an expression in x and y and the grapher draws a field of short segments, each with the slope the equation gives at that point. Add a starting point after a comma, as in dy/dx = x - y, y(0) = 1, and it also draws the solution curve through that point, in both directions, computed numerically with the Runge-Kutta method. The default does exactly that: watch the solution settle onto the line y = x - 1. A letter such as k in dy/dx = k*y becomes a slider, and the segments sit on a grid of 1, 2 or 5 units (like the grid lines), so zooming in adds more segments and zooming out spaces them wider.
points: Write dy/dx = f(x, y); the right side can use x, y and sliders.
Add , y(x0) = y0 to draw the solution curve through that starting point.
Each segment has the true slope: where it is flat the slope is 0, and where it is vertical the slope is undefined.
Solution curves follow the segments and never cross one another.
Zoom in for a denser field or out for a wider one: the spacing follows the grid lines.
The solution curve is a numerical approximation, so use it to check a sketch or a hand solution.

examples.l: Exponential growth: the solution is e^x
Slope depends on both x and y; the solution is e^(x^2/2)
Logistic growth leveling off at the equilibrium y = 4
Slider k: growth for k > 0 and decay for k < 0
The solution is the upper half of the circle x^2 + y^2 = 4

faq.q: Does this tool draw a slope field?
faq.a: Yes. Type dy/dx = and an expression in x and y, such as dy/dx = x - y. Short segments show the slope at each point, and a starting point such as y(0) = 1 adds the solution curve through it.

faq.q: How do I find the solution through a given point?
faq.a: Add the point after a comma: dy/dx = y, y(0) = 2. The solution curve is drawn through it in both directions. To do it by hand, find the general solution with a constant C and substitute the point to solve for C.

faq.q: What is an equilibrium solution?
faq.a: It is a constant solution where the slope is zero everywhere on the line. For dy/dx = y*(1 - y/4), y = 0 and y = 4 are equilibria, and you can see flat segments along both lines.

faq.q: Why do solution curves never cross?
faq.a: If two solutions met at a point, the equation would give two different slopes there, contradicting the single slope at each point. This is why solution curves fan out in order.

faq.q: How do I match a slope field to its equation?
faq.a: Check where the slopes are zero, where they are steep and whether they depend on x, y or both. Then type your guess and compare the picture with the one in your problem.

worked.title: Exponential growth from dy/dx = y
worked.problem: Solve dy/dx = y with y(0) = 1 and read the slope field.
steps: Every slope equals the y-value, so the segments are flat on y = 0 and steeper higher up.
Separate variables: dy/y = dx, so ln|y| = x + C, and y = Ce^x.
Use y(0) = 1: C = 1, so y = e^x.
Check against the field: at (1, e) the slope should be e ≈ 2.718, and the solution passes through that point.
worked.answer: y = e^x. The solution curve follows the segments and has y(1) = e ≈ 2.718.

worked.title: A circle from dy/dx = −x/y
worked.problem: Solve dy/dx = −x/y with y(0) = 2.
steps: Separate variables: y dy = −x dx.
Integrate: y²/2 = −x²/2 + C, so x² + y² = 2C.
Use y(0) = 2: 0 + 4 = 2C, so x² + y² = 4.
Since y(0) = 2 is positive, the solution is the upper half: y = √(4 − x²). At (1, √3) the slope is −1/√3 ≈ −0.577.
worked.answer: y = √(4 − x²), the upper half of a circle of radius 2. The slope segments are always perpendicular to the radius.

pages.title: Taylor Polynomial Calculator & Grapher | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Compare sin(x) or eˣ with Taylor polynomial approximations on one graph. A free online Taylor series grapher for AP Calculus BC and college.
intro: A Taylor polynomial approximates a function near a chosen point using its derivatives. The more terms you include, the better the polynomial hugs the original curve and the farther from the center the match extends. Taylor series are how calculators compute sine, cosine and exponentials, and they are a standard topic in AP Calculus BC and college calculus.

This grapher does not generate the polynomial, so you type the function and its approximation yourself. The default pair is sin(x) and x - x^3/6 + x^5/120, the degree-5 polynomial centered at 0. Near the origin the two curves are almost indistinguishable, then they separate as x grows. Add terms one at a time to see the match widen, which makes the idea of error and radius of convergence much easier to understand.
points: A Taylor polynomial of degree n centered at 0 uses f(0), f'(0), and so on up to the n-th derivative.
Each added term improves the match over a wider interval around the center.
Functions like sin x, cos x and e^x are matched everywhere eventually; ln(1 + x) and 1/(1 - x) only work for |x| < 1.
The error of an approximation grows as you move away from the center.

examples.l: Pair with 1 + x + x^2/2 + x^3/6 to see the degree-3 fit
Pair with 1 - x^2/2 + x^4/24, an even polynomial for an even function
Pair with x - x^2/2 + x^3/3; notice it fails past x = 1
Pair with 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 to see the radius of convergence

faq.q: Does this calculator generate the Taylor polynomial for me?
faq.a: No. You type the polynomial from the series you learned or computed. Then the graph shows how well it matches, which is a quick check on your coefficients.

faq.q: What is a Maclaurin series?
faq.a: It is a Taylor series centered at 0. The examples on this page, such as sin x and e^x, are all Maclaurin series.

faq.q: What does the radius of convergence mean?
faq.a: It is how far from the center the series still converges to the function. For e^x it is infinite, but for 1/(1 - x) it is 1, which is why the polynomial drifts away from the curve beyond x = 1.

faq.q: Why do odd functions only have odd powers?
faq.a: Because the polynomial must have the same symmetry as the function. sin x is odd, so its series uses x, x^3, x^5 and so on, while cos x is even and uses only even powers.

faq.q: How many terms do I need for a good approximation?
faq.a: It depends on how far from the center you need accuracy. Add terms and zoom in; when the two curves are indistinguishable across your interval, you have enough.

worked.title: How good is the degree-5 sine polynomial?
worked.problem: Use sin x ≈ x − x³/6 + x⁵/120 to estimate sin 1 and find the error.
steps: The calculator value is sin 1 = 0.841471.
worked.answer: The estimate 0.84167 is within 0.0002 of sin 1. Graph both curves: they overlap near x = 0 and drift apart as |x| grows.

worked.title: A polynomial that only works on part of the domain
worked.problem: Approximate ln(1 + x) with x − x²/2 + x³/3 and test it at x = 0.5.
steps: ln(1.5) = 0.405465, so the error is about 0.011.
The series for ln(1 + x) converges only for −1 < x ≤ 1. Graph both curves: the polynomial is accurate near 0 and goes wrong near x = −1, where ln(1 + x) drops to −∞.
worked.answer: At x = 0.5 the three-term polynomial gives 0.4167 against the true 0.4055.

pages.title: Normal Distribution Grapher (Bell Curve) | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph the normal distribution and see how the mean and standard deviation reshape the bell curve. A free online normal curve plotter.
intro: The normal distribution is the symmetric bell-shaped curve that describes heights, test scores, measurement error and many other quantities. It is completely determined by two numbers, the mean, which sets the center, and the standard deviation, which sets the spread. The curve is highest at the mean and falls away equally on both sides, so about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation, 95% within two and 99.7% within three.

Graph the density function f(x) = (1/(s*sqrt(2*pi))) * exp(-0.5*((x - m)/s)^2) to see the effect of each parameter. The default curve is the standard normal with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Change the center by replacing x with x - 2 inside the exponent, or widen the curve by increasing s. Add a vertical line such as x = 1.96 to mark the cutoff that leaves 2.5% in the right tail.
points: The mean m shifts the curve left or right without changing its shape.
The standard deviation s stretches the curve: a larger s gives a lower, wider bell.
The total area under every normal curve is 1, so a wider curve must be shorter.
The empirical rule: roughly 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.

examples.l: Mean 0 with the standard deviation s as a slider: drag it to widen or narrow
Mean 2, standard deviation 1
Mean 0, standard deviation 2: wider and lower
Vertical line at z = 1.96, the cutoff for a 95% interval

faq.q: What is the formula for the normal curve?
faq.a: f(x) = (1/(s*sqrt(2*pi))) * e^(-(x - m)^2/(2*s^2)), where m is the mean and s is the standard deviation. The grapher accepts this as typed, using exp(...) for e to a power.

faq.q: What is the standard normal distribution?
faq.a: It is the normal curve with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Any normal value can be converted to it with a z-score, z = (x - m)/s, which tells you how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.

faq.q: Why is the peak of a wider curve lower?
faq.a: Because the area under any density curve is always 1. If the curve spreads out sideways it has to drop in height to keep the same total area.

faq.q: Can this find probabilities?
faq.a: This page draws the curve and marks values you choose, but it does not give areas. For a probability from a z-score, use a z-table, or the z-score calculator on this site to get z first.

faq.q: Is real data ever exactly normal?
faq.a: Rarely. The normal curve is a model that fits many measurements well, especially averages, thanks to the central limit theorem, but it should be checked against the actual data.

worked.title: Peak and inflection of the standard normal
worked.problem: Find the height of the standard normal curve at its peak and where it changes curvature.
steps: f(x) = (1/sqrt(2pi)) e^(-x^2/2). At x = 0 the height is 1/sqrt(2pi), about 0.3989.
The curve changes from bending down to bending up at one standard deviation from the mean, x = -1 and x = 1.
worked.answer: Peak about 0.3989 at x = 0; inflection points at x = -1 and x = 1.

worked.title: Shift and stretch
worked.problem: Graph a normal curve with mean 1 and standard deviation 2. What is its peak?
steps: The center moves to x = 1. The peak height is 1/(2 sqrt(2pi)), about 0.1995, half the standard normal peak.
A larger standard deviation spreads the curve out and lowers it, because the total area stays 1.
worked.answer: Peak about 0.1995 at x = 1; inflection points at x = -1 and x = 3.

pages.title: Bell Curve Generator (Mean & Std Dev) | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Generate a bell curve from any mean and standard deviation and compare spreads side by side with this free online bell curve maker.
intro: A bell curve is the everyday name for a normal distribution, and generating one only takes a mean and a standard deviation. Teachers use bell curves to talk about grade distributions, researchers use them to describe measurements, and students meet them in statistics when learning z-scores, the empirical rule and confidence intervals.

To generate your own, replace the mean and spread in the formula (1/(s*sqrt(2*pi))) * exp(-0.5*((x - m)/s)^2). The default curve has mean 1 and standard deviation 1, so its peak sits at x = 1 with a height of about 0.4. Add a second curve with a different standard deviation to compare spreads on the same axes. Because the total area is the same, a larger spread always gives a shorter and wider bell. Use the sliders in the examples to adjust both values and watch the shape change.
points: The peak of the bell is at the mean, and the curve is symmetric around it.
Two curves with the same mean but different standard deviations share a center and differ in width.
Two curves with the same standard deviation but different means have the same shape in different places.
The inflection points, where the curve changes from bending down to bending up, sit one standard deviation from the mean.

examples.l: Full bell curve with sliders for mean m and spread s
Mean 1, standard deviation 0.5: narrow and tall
Mean 1, standard deviation 2: wide and short
Vertical line two standard deviations above the mean when the mean is 1 and s = 1: a cutoff marker

faq.q: What do I need to generate a bell curve?
faq.a: Just a mean and a standard deviation. Put the mean where the peak should be and the standard deviation as the spread, then type the formula or use the slider version.

faq.q: What does grading on a curve mean?
faq.a: Usually it means adjusting scores so they follow a bell-shaped pattern or shifting them by a fixed amount. Policies differ by teacher and school, so ask your instructor what they use.

faq.q: How do I compare two bell curves?
faq.a: Graph both on the same axes. Same mean with different spreads look nested, while different means with the same spread look like copies shifted sideways.

faq.q: What is the area under the curve?
faq.a: It is always 1, because it represents total probability. A specific area between two x-values is the probability that a value falls in that interval.

faq.q: Why does my curve look small on the screen?
faq.a: Peak heights are about 0.4 divided by the standard deviation, which is small compared with the x-axis. Zoom in on the y-axis or use the home button to reset the view.

worked.title: Narrow versus wide
worked.problem: Compare bell curves with standard deviations 0.5 and 2 (mean 0).
steps: Peak height is 1/(sigma sqrt(2pi)). For sigma = 0.5 that is about 0.7979, and for sigma = 2 it is about 0.1995.
Making the standard deviation four times larger makes the peak four times lower.
worked.answer: Peaks about 0.798 (sigma 0.5) and 0.199 (sigma 2). Both have total area 1.

worked.title: The 95% rule
worked.problem: What share of a normal distribution lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean?
steps: Within 2 standard deviations means z between -2 and 2.
The area to the left of 2 is about 0.9772 and to the left of -2 about 0.0228, so the area between is about 0.9545.
worked.answer: About 95.45% (often rounded to 95%).

pages.title: Supply and Demand Grapher (Equilibrium) | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph supply and demand curves and find the equilibrium price and quantity where they meet. A free online grapher for economics class.
intro: Supply and demand is the basic model economists use to explain prices. Demand slopes downward because people buy less as the price rises, and supply slopes upward because producers offer more as the price rises. The point where the curves cross is the market equilibrium, where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer.

On this grapher the horizontal axis is quantity and the vertical axis is price. The default demand curve is y = -0.7x + 8.5 and the supply curve is y = 0.8x + 1. They cross at x = 5, y = 5, so the equilibrium quantity is 5 and the equilibrium price is 5. Change the intercept or slope of either line to model a shift: a tax moves supply up, and a rise in income can move demand to the right. The intersection updates in the Key points panel.
points: Quantity is on the x-axis and price on the y-axis; the lines are written as price in terms of quantity.
Equilibrium is where supply and demand intersect, and it appears under Key points.
A shift of a curve changes the equilibrium; a movement along a curve is a response to price.
A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage, and a price floor above equilibrium creates a surplus.

examples.l: Supply after a per-unit tax of 1: equilibrium moves to about quantity 4.3, price 5.5
Demand after an increase: equilibrium rises to quantity 6, price 5.8
Price ceiling at 4: supply gives about 3.75 units and demand wants about 6.4, a shortage
Price floor at 7: compare the quantity on each curve to find the surplus

faq.q: How do I find the equilibrium price and quantity?
faq.a: Set the supply and demand equations equal and solve for x, then substitute to get y. Here 0.8x + 1 = -0.7x + 8.5 gives x = 5 and y = 5, and the graph marks the same point.

faq.q: What causes a shift in demand or supply?
faq.a: Changes other than the price itself, such as income, tastes, input costs, taxes or technology. Change the intercept of a line to shift it, and change the slope to alter how sensitive quantity is to price.

faq.q: What is a shortage or a surplus?
faq.a: A shortage means quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price, and a surplus means the opposite. Draw a horizontal line at that price and compare where it meets each curve.

faq.q: Why are the numbers so small?
faq.a: They are illustrative. Real markets use units such as dollars and thousands of items, but the shapes and the logic are the same, and small numbers keep the graph readable.

faq.q: Is this meant for economics exams?
faq.a: It is a study aid for AP Micro, AP Macro and intro economics. Real exam graphs follow your course materials, so use it to understand shifts, not as official policy guidance.

worked.title: Find the equilibrium
worked.problem: Supply is P = 0.8Q + 1 and demand is P = -0.7Q + 8.5. Find the equilibrium.
steps: Set supply equal to demand: 0.8Q + 1 = -0.7Q + 8.5, so 1.5Q = 7.5 and Q = 5.
Then P = 0.8(5) + 1 = 5. Check in demand: -0.7(5) + 8.5 = 5.
worked.answer: Equilibrium quantity 5 at price 5.

worked.title: A price ceiling
worked.problem: Add a price ceiling at P = 4. What happens?
steps: Suppliers offer 0.8Q + 1 = 4, so Q = 3.75.
Buyers want -0.7Q + 8.5 = 4, so Q = 4.5/0.7, about 6.43.
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by about 6.43 - 3.75 = 2.68 units.
worked.answer: A shortage of about 2.68 units.

pages.title: Projectile Motion Grapher (Trajectory) | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Graph a projectile's parabolic path, height versus distance, and adjust the equation to explore launch angle and speed. Free physics plotter.
intro: A projectile launched at an angle follows a parabola. Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal motion is steady while gravity bends the vertical motion, and eliminating time gives height as a quadratic in the horizontal distance. The path is y = x tan(a) - g x^2/(2 v^2 cos^2(a)) for launch speed v and angle a, with g about 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth.

The default graph, y = x - 0.1x^2, is a simple example in meters. It starts at the origin, peaks at x = 5 with a height of 2.5 and lands at x = 10. That matches a 45 degree launch at roughly 9.9 m/s. The peak height and range appear in Key points as the vertex and the second root. Use the slider version below to explore how speed and angle change the shape, and remember that real projectiles with drag fall short of this idealized curve.
points: The path is a parabola: horizontal distance is on the x-axis and height on the y-axis.
The roots are the launch point and the landing point; the vertex is the maximum height.
At a fixed speed, a 45 degree launch gives the longest range on level ground.
Complementary angles, such as 30 and 60 degrees, give the same range with different heights.

examples.l: Steeper launch: peak 10 at x = 10, lands at x = 20
Faster launch at 45 degrees: peak 5 at x = 10, range 20
Full formula with sliders for angle a and speed v (set the angle chip to DEG)
A wall or net of height 3: where does the path cross it?

faq.q: What is the formula for projectile motion?
faq.a: With no air resistance, y = x tan(a) - g x^2/(2 v^2 cos^2(a)). The range on level ground is v^2 sin(2a)/g and the maximum height is v^2 sin^2(a)/(2g).

faq.q: How do I find the range from the graph?
faq.a: Read the positive root of the parabola, the point where the height returns to zero. It is listed under Key points as a root.

faq.q: Why does 45 degrees give the maximum range?
faq.a: Because range is proportional to sin(2a), which is largest when 2a = 90 degrees. Try the slider with angles of 30, 45 and 60 and compare the landing point.

faq.q: Does this include air resistance?
faq.a: No. It is the ideal textbook model. Real paths are shorter and more lopsided because of drag, which this curve does not capture.

faq.q: How do I switch between degrees and radians?
faq.a: Tap the RAD/DEG chip next to the equations. The slider formula expects degrees if you want to use angles like 45 or 60.

worked.title: Range and maximum height
worked.problem: A path is modeled by y = x - 0.1x^2 (x is horizontal distance). Find the range and maximum height.
steps: Landing is where y = 0: x(1 - 0.1x) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 10. The range is 10.
The parabola is symmetric, so the top is at x = 5: y = 5 - 0.1(25) = 2.5.
worked.answer: Range 10 and maximum height 2.5.

worked.title: Compare two launches
worked.problem: Compare y = x - 0.1x^2 with y = x - 0.05x^2.
steps: For y = x - 0.05x^2, landing is at x = 20 and the top is at x = 10: y = 10 - 5 = 5.
Halving the x^2 coefficient doubled both the range and the peak height, from (10, 2.5) to (20, 5).
At x = 15 the second path is at 15 - 11.25 = 3.75.
worked.answer: The second path goes twice as far (20) and twice as high (5).

pages.title: Z-Score Calculator: Percentile & Probability | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free z-score calculator. Convert a value to a z-score, find a value from z or a percentile, and get normal-curve probabilities with a shaded bell curve.
intro: A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean. Positive means above the mean, negative means below, and zero means exactly average. This calculator converts a raw value to a z-score, turns a z-score or percentile back into a value, and finds the probability (area under the normal curve) for one tail, a middle range or both tails.
It assumes the data is roughly normal, which is the usual setting for z-score and percentile questions in AP Statistics and introductory college statistics.

p: z = (x − μ) / σ, where x is the value, μ is the mean and σ is the standard deviation. To go back from a z-score to a value, use x = μ + zσ. If you only have a sample, the same formula works with the sample mean and sample standard deviation.

A test has a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 10. A score of 85 gives z = (85 − 70) / 10 = 1.5. The area to the left of z = 1.5 is about 0.9332, so the score is at about the 93rd percentile and roughly 6.7% of scores are higher. The calculator opens with these numbers already filled in.

ul: Left tail, P(X < a): the share of values below a. This is the percentile.
Right tail, P(X > a): the share of values above a.
Between a and b: the probability that a value falls inside the range.
Outside a and b: the probability in both tails together, which is what two-sided tests use.

p: In a normal distribution about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean (z between −1 and 1), about 95% within 2, and about 99.7% within 3. That is why values beyond z = ±2 are called unusual and beyond ±3 are rare.

ul: z = 1.645 is the 95th percentile (a 5% right tail).
z = 1.96 is the 97.5th percentile and marks the middle 95%.
z = 2.576 is the 99.5th percentile and marks the middle 99%.
Scores have mean 100 and standard deviation 15. A score of 130 gives z = (130 - 100)/15 = 2. The area to the left is about 0.9772, so it is near the 98th percentile.
What share of scores fall between 85 and 115? Those are z = -1 and z = 1, which hold about 0.6827 (68.27%) of a normal distribution.
A test has mean 70 and standard deviation 10. What score marks the 90th percentile? The 90th percentile is z of about 1.2816, so x = 70 + 1.2816(10), about 82.8.
Using the wrong standard deviation. Use the population value if you know it, and the sample value otherwise.
Dropping the sign. A negative z-score means the value is below the mean, so the left tail is smaller than 0.5.
Reading a z-score as a probability. The z-score is a distance; the probability is the area under the curve at that distance.
Using normal-curve areas on strongly skewed data. A z-score is still computable, but the percentile from the normal table will not be accurate.

faq.q: What is a good z-score?
faq.a: It depends on what you are measuring. A z-score only says how far a value is from the mean. For test scores a high positive z means a high percentile, while for something like error rates a low or negative z is better. In a normal distribution, values beyond ±2 are unusual and beyond ±3 are rare.

faq.q: Can a z-score be negative?
faq.a: Yes. A negative z-score means the value is below the mean. A z-score of −1.2 is 1.2 standard deviations below average.

faq.q: How do I find a z-score from a percentile?
faq.a: Choose “Z-score and value from a percentile”, then enter the percentile. For example, the 90th percentile is z ≈ 1.2816.

faq.q: What is the difference between a z-score and a t-score?
faq.a: A z-score uses the normal distribution, normally with a known or assumed standard deviation. A t statistic uses the sample standard deviation and the t distribution, which has heavier tails when the sample is small. For tests on means from small samples, use the t-test calculator.

faq.q: Does it work if my data is not normal?
faq.a: You can always compute a z-score, but the probabilities and percentiles assume a normal distribution. For skewed data they can be misleading, so check a histogram first.

faq.q: Is a z-score the same as a standard score?
faq.a: Yes. Standard score and z-score mean the same thing: the number of standard deviations a value is from the mean.

pages.title: Standard Deviation Calculator with Steps | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free standard deviation calculator. Paste your data for sample and population SD, variance, mean, standard error and a step-by-step table.
intro: Standard deviation measures how spread out numbers are around their mean. A small value means the data sits close to the average, and a large value means it is more spread out. Paste your numbers and this calculator returns the sample and population versions, plus variance, mean, median, range, standard error and a step-by-step table of deviations.

p: Use population standard deviation (divide by n) when your numbers are the whole group you care about, such as every score in a class of 25. Use sample standard deviation (divide by n − 1) when your numbers are a sample from a larger group and you want to estimate that group's spread. Dividing by n − 1 is called Bessel's correction. Most statistics courses expect the sample formula unless the problem says the data is a population.

ul: Mean: x̄ = Σx / n
Sample variance: s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)
Population variance: σ² = Σ(x − μ)² / N
Standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
Standard error of the mean: s / √n

p: For 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 7, 9, 5 the mean is 47 / 8 = 5.875 and the sum of squared deviations is 28.875. The sample variance is 28.875 / 7 = 4.125, so the sample standard deviation is about 2.031. The population variance is 28.875 / 8 = 3.609, so the population standard deviation is about 1.900. The calculator opens with this data.

sections.h: What a standard deviation tells you
p: Standard deviation is in the same units as your data, unlike variance, which is in squared units. In a roughly normal data set about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two. Because every value is squared in the calculation, outliers have a large effect, so check for extreme values.
Find the standard deviation of 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 7. The mean is 33/6 = 5.5. The squared deviations are 2.25, 6.25, 0.25, 0.25, 6.25 and 2.25, which add to 17.5.

Sample variance = 17.5/5 = 3.5, so the sample standard deviation is about 1.871. Population variance = 17.5/6, about 2.917, so the population standard deviation is about 1.708. Paste the six numbers into the calculator to confirm both.

sections.h: How one outlier changes the answer
p: Add the value 40 to the list above. The mean jumps from 5.5 to about 10.43 and the sample standard deviation from about 1.87 to about 13.15. A single extreme value can multiply the spread, which is why standard deviation is paired with a plot or the median and quartiles when data may contain outliers.

ul: Dividing by n when the data is a sample. Use n - 1 for a sample.
Forgetting to take the square root, which gives the variance instead.
Mixing units. The standard deviation has the same units as the data; the variance has squared units.

faq.q: What is the difference between variance and standard deviation?
faq.a: Variance is the average squared distance from the mean. Standard deviation is its square root, which puts the spread back into the original units of the data.

faq.q: Can standard deviation be negative?
faq.a: No. It is a square root, so it is zero or positive. It is zero only when every value in the data set is identical.

faq.q: How many numbers do I need?
faq.a: At least 2 for a sample standard deviation, because the formula divides by n − 1. Larger samples give more reliable estimates.

faq.q: What is the difference between standard deviation and standard error?
faq.a: Standard deviation describes how spread out individual values are. Standard error of the mean (s divided by the square root of n) describes how much the sample mean would vary from sample to sample.

faq.q: How do outliers affect the result?
faq.a: A single extreme value can increase the standard deviation a lot. If your data has outliers, also look at the median and the range, or use a measure such as the interquartile range.

faq.q: Can I paste data from a spreadsheet?
faq.a: Yes. Copy a column from Excel or Google Sheets and paste it in. Numbers can be separated by commas, spaces or new lines, and negative numbers and decimals work.

pages.title: Confidence Interval Calculator | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free confidence interval calculator for a mean (t or z) or a proportion (Wilson and Wald). See margin of error, critical value and a shaded graph.
intro: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter based on a sample. This calculator builds an interval for a population mean from a sample mean, standard deviation and sample size, or for a proportion from a count of successes. Choose 90%, 95%, 99% or your own confidence level.

ul: Mean, σ unknown: x̄ ± t* · s/√n, with n − 1 degrees of freedom
Mean, σ known: x̄ ± z* · σ/√n
Proportion, Wald: p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n)
Proportion, Wilson: re-centres and adjusts the width, and works better for small samples or proportions near 0 or 1.

p: A sample of n = 36 has a mean of 52.4 and a standard deviation of 6.8. The standard error is 6.8 / 6 = 1.133. For 95% confidence with 35 degrees of freedom, t* is about 2.030, so the margin of error is about 2.30 and the interval is about (50.10, 54.70). The calculator opens with these numbers.

Use t when the population standard deviation is unknown, which is almost always the case with real data. Use z only when the population standard deviation is known from outside your sample. With large samples the two give nearly the same answer.

sections.h: How to read a confidence interval
p: A 95% confidence interval does not mean there is a 95% chance the true value lies inside this one interval. It means that if you repeated the sampling many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true value.

ul: 90% confidence: z* = 1.645
95% confidence: z* = 1.960
99% confidence: z* = 2.576

A sample of n = 36 has mean 50 and s = 12. The standard error is 12/6 = 2. With 35 degrees of freedom the 95% critical value is about 2.030, so the margin of error is about 4.06 and the interval is about 45.94 to 54.06.

In a poll, 120 of 200 people say yes, so the sample proportion is 0.6. The standard error is sqrt(0.6 x 0.4/200), about 0.0346, and the 95% margin of error is 1.96 x 0.0346, about 0.068. The interval is about 0.532 to 0.668.
How many people give a 95% margin of error of 0.03 when you have no estimate of p? Use p = 0.5: n = (1.96/0.03)^2 x 0.25, about 1067.1, so round up to 1068.
Saying there is a 95% probability that the true mean is in this particular interval. The 95% describes the method: about 95% of intervals built this way capture the true value.
Using z instead of t with a small sample and an estimated standard deviation.
Forgetting to round the required sample size up.

faq.q: What is the margin of error?
faq.a: It is the critical value times the standard error, which is the distance from the sample estimate to each end of the interval.

faq.q: How can I get a narrower interval?
faq.a: Use a larger sample or a lower confidence level. Quadrupling the sample size roughly halves the margin of error.

faq.q: Is a 99% interval better than a 95% interval?
faq.a: It is more likely to contain the true value, but it is wider and so less precise. The right level depends on how costly a miss would be.

faq.q: Which proportion interval should I use?
faq.a: Many textbooks teach the Wald (normal approximation) interval, so it is shown for checking homework. The Wilson interval is generally more reliable, especially when n is small or the proportion is near 0 or 1.

faq.q: What conditions do I need?
faq.a: The sample should be random and the observations independent. For a mean, the data should be roughly normal or the sample reasonably large. For a proportion, a common rule of thumb is at least 10 successes and 10 failures.

faq.q: What if I only have raw data?
faq.a: Paste your numbers into the standard deviation calculator to get the mean, standard deviation and n, then enter them here.

pages.title: T-Test Calculator: One-Sample, Two-Sample | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free t-test calculator. Run a one-sample, Welch, pooled or paired t-test from raw data or summary statistics and get t, df, p-value and a graph.
intro: A t-test checks whether a sample mean differs from a value, or whether two means differ, when the population standard deviation is unknown. Choose the test type, enter raw data or summary statistics, and the calculator returns the t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, a confidence interval and an effect size, with a shaded graph of the p-value.

ul: One-sample: compare one sample mean to a known or claimed value.
Two-sample (Welch): compare the means of two independent groups without assuming equal variances. This is the safer default.
Two-sample (pooled): the same comparison, but it assumes both groups have the same variance, and uses n₁ + n₂ − 2 degrees of freedom.
Paired: compare two measurements on the same subjects, such as before and after. The test runs on the differences.
One-sample: t = (x̄ − μ₀) / (s/√n), with n − 1 degrees of freedom
Welch: t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂), with Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
Paired: t = d̄ / (sᵈ/√n), where d is each pair's difference

p: Sample 1 is 23, 25, 28, 30, 26, 27, 24, 29 (mean 26.5) and sample 2 is 20, 22, 25, 24, 21, 23, 26, 22 (mean 22.875). A Welch two-sample test gives t ≈ 3.22 with about 13.5 degrees of freedom and a two-sided p-value of about 0.0064. At α = 0.05 that is enough to reject the null hypothesis that the means are equal. The calculator opens with this data.

The p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting a t statistic at least as extreme as yours. A p-value below your significance level α is evidence against the null hypothesis. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and a non-significant result does not prove the means are equal.

ul: Observations are independent (or properly paired).
The data is roughly normal, or the samples are reasonably large.
There are no extreme outliers. Plot your data if you are unsure.

p: Six students take a quiz before and after a review session. Before: 72, 75, 68, 80, 77, 71. After: 78, 79, 70, 85, 80, 75. The differences are 6, 4, 2, 5, 3, 4, with mean 4 and standard deviation about 1.414.

The standard error is 1.414/sqrt(6), about 0.577, so t = 4/0.577, about 6.93 with 5 degrees of freedom. The two-sided p-value is about 0.00096, strong evidence that scores changed. Enter the two lists in the paired test to see the same result.

ul: Using a two-sample test on paired data. If the same people are measured twice, use the paired test.
Choosing a one-tailed test after seeing which way the data points. Decide the direction before collecting data.
Reading a large p-value as proof of no difference. It only means the data did not give enough evidence.
Ignoring a very small sample with strong skew or outliers, where the t-test can mislead.

faq.q: Should I use Welch or the pooled t-test?
faq.a: Welch is the safer choice because it does not assume equal variances and loses little power when the variances are equal. Use the pooled test when your course or problem tells you to assume equal variances.

faq.q: When do I use a one-tailed test?
faq.a: Only when your hypothesis names a direction before you look at the data, such as “the new method scores higher”. Otherwise use the two-sided test.

faq.q: What are degrees of freedom?
faq.a: They describe how much independent information the standard deviation estimate rests on. For a one-sample or paired test it is n − 1. The Welch test uses a fractional value.

faq.q: What does Cohen's d mean?
faq.a: It is an effect size: the difference between means in standard deviation units. As a rough guide, 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium and 0.8 is large, but what counts as large depends on the field.

faq.q: Can I use a t-test on a small sample?
faq.a: Yes, if the data is roughly normal. With very small samples the test is sensitive to outliers and skew.

faq.q: Why does the paired test need two lists of the same length?
faq.a: Each value in the first list is matched with the value in the same position in the second list, and the test runs on those differences.

pages.title: Chi-Square Calculator: Fit & Independence | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free chi-square calculator. Run a goodness-of-fit or independence test, get χ², degrees of freedom, p-value, expected counts and a shaded graph.
intro: A chi-square test compares counts. The goodness-of-fit test asks whether observed counts match an expected distribution, such as whether a die is fair. The test of independence asks whether two categorical variables are related, using a table of counts. Enter your counts and the calculator returns the chi-square statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, expected counts, each cell's contribution and a shaded graph of the p-value.

sections.h: Which chi-square test do I need?
ul: Goodness of fit: one categorical variable, compared with an expected distribution. Degrees of freedom = categories − 1.
Test of independence: two categorical variables in a contingency table. Degrees of freedom = (rows − 1) × (columns − 1).
Chi-square statistic: χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E, where O is the observed count and E is the expected count
Independence, expected count: E = (row total × column total) / grand total
Cramér’s V (effect size for a table): √(χ² / (n × min(rows − 1, columns − 1)))

sections.h: Worked example: is a die fair?
p: A die is rolled 60 times and the six faces come up 5, 8, 9, 8, 10 and 20 times. If the die is fair, each face is expected 10 times. The contributions (O − E)² / E are 2.5, 0.4, 0.1, 0.4, 0 and 10, so χ² = 13.4 with 5 degrees of freedom and a p-value of about 0.0199. At α = 0.05 you reject the idea that the die is fair. The calculator opens with these counts.

sections.h: Worked example: independence in a 2 × 2 table
p: Switch to the test of independence and use the table 30, 20 / 20, 30. Every expected count is 25, so χ² = 4 × (5² / 25) = 4 with 1 degree of freedom, giving p ≈ 0.0455.

ul: Use counts, not percentages or averages.
Observations are independent and come from a random sample.
Each expected count should be at least 5. The calculator warns you when it is not.

p: A game spinner has five equal sections. In 100 spins the counts are 18, 22, 20, 25 and 15. If the spinner is fair each section is expected 20 times.

The statistic is (18-20)^2/20 + (22-20)^2/20 + 0 + (25-20)^2/20 + (15-20)^2/20 = (4 + 4 + 0 + 25 + 25)/20 = 2.9, with 5 - 1 = 4 degrees of freedom. The p-value is about 0.575, so these counts are consistent with a fair spinner.

ul: Entering percentages instead of counts. The test needs raw counts.
Using a chi-square test on repeated measures of the same people, which breaks independence.
Forgetting that a significant result says the categories are related, not why.

faq.q: What does the p-value tell me?
faq.a: It is the probability, if the null hypothesis is true, of getting a chi-square statistic at least as large as yours. A p-value below your significance level is evidence against the null hypothesis. It does not tell you how strong or important the effect is.

faq.q: Can the chi-square statistic be negative?
faq.a: No. Every term (O − E)² / E is zero or positive, so the statistic is zero or positive. Large values mean the observed counts are far from the expected ones.

faq.q: What if some expected counts are below 5?
faq.a: The chi-square approximation becomes less reliable. Combine categories where that makes sense, collect more data, or use an exact test such as Fisher's exact test for a 2 × 2 table.

faq.q: Does it use the Yates continuity correction?
faq.a: No. It uses the standard formula taught in most courses. Some software applies a continuity correction to 2 × 2 tables by default, which gives a slightly different p-value.

faq.q: Can I enter percentages?
faq.a: For the independence test, enter counts. For goodness of fit, enter observed counts, and you can give the expected distribution as proportions or percentages in the custom proportions option.

faq.q: What does Cramér's V mean?
faq.a: It measures how strongly two variables are associated in a table, from 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect association). It helps because a large sample can make a tiny effect statistically significant.

pages.h1: TI-83 Plus vs. TI-84 Plus Comparison
intro: The TI-83 Plus and TI-84 Plus are close relatives from the same product family, and for years they were the default graphing calculators in US classrooms. The TI-84 Plus came later with a faster processor, more memory, a USB connection and a built-in clock, but the two share the same basic menus and key layout. Most graphing, table and regression steps you learn on one carry over to the other.

If you are choosing between them for a class, check what your teacher recommends and which models your tests allow, because test policies change. If you only need to practice graphing at home, a free online calculator can cover a lot of the same ground. The default graph here, x^2 - 5 and 2x + 1, shows a typical task: finding where a parabola and a line intersect, which both calculators do with a calculate-intersect menu and this page does automatically.
points: Speed and memory: the TI-84 Plus is the faster one and holds more apps and programs.
Same workflow: Y= for equations, GRAPH to plot, TABLE for values, STAT for regression.
Exam rules: both have historically been accepted on many US tests, but check the current policy for each test.
Online graphing is good for practice and homework, but it is not a substitute for an approved device on a test that requires one.

examples.l: Y1 on a TI-83 or TI-84; the roots appear under Key points
Y2: where it meets Y1 matches the calculate-intersect result
Use for a zero/root practice problem and compare with factoring
Plot points like the STAT PLOT feature

faq.q: What is the main difference between a TI-83 Plus and a TI-84 Plus?
faq.a: The TI-84 Plus is the newer model with a faster processor, more storage memory and USB connectivity. The basic graphing and statistics features are very similar.

faq.q: Can I use a TI-84 Plus on standardized tests?
faq.a: Many US tests have allowed it historically, but policies change and differ by test. Check the current calculator policy for the exact test you will take.

faq.q: Are TI-83 Plus programs compatible with the TI-84 Plus?
faq.a: Many are, but not all, because the models differ in hardware. If a program matters to you, test it on the model your class uses.

faq.q: Do I still need a physical calculator if I use ExamGrapher?
faq.a: That depends on your class and exams. This site is independent of Texas Instruments and is best used for practice, checking work and learning graphing skills.

faq.q: How do I find an intersection on each calculator?
faq.a: On the TI-83/84 use 2nd, TRACE (CALC), then intersect and confirm three prompts. Here, just enter both equations and read the marked intersection under Key points.

worked.title: Intersection of a parabola and a line
worked.problem: Find where y = x² − 5 and y = 2x + 1 meet.
steps: Set x² − 5 = 2x + 1, so x² − 2x − 6 = 0.
Quadratic formula: x = (2 ± √(4 + 24))/2 = 1 ± √7.
On either TI: Y= for both equations, GRAPH, then 2nd TRACE 5:intersect and answer the three prompts for each point.
worked.answer: Intersections at about (3.646, 8.292) and (−1.646, −2.292). The keystrokes are the same on the TI-83 Plus and the TI-84 Plus.

worked.problem: Find the line of best fit for (1, 2), (2, 4.1), (3, 5.9).

Here: type the points or paste them into Data table & regression and choose Linear.
worked.answer: y = 1.95x + 0.1 with r ≈ 0.999 on all three.

worked.title: Is this table exponential? Build the model
worked.problem: A table gives y = 50, 40, 32, 25.6 for x = 0, 1, 2, 3. Find a model and predict y at x = 5.
steps: Check for a constant ratio: 40/50 = 0.8, 32/40 = 0.8 and 25.6/32 = 0.8.

pages.h1: How to Solve Equations by Graphing
intro: Solving an equation by graphing means turning each side into its own graph and finding where they meet. The x-coordinates of the intersection points are the solutions. This works for equations that are hard or impossible to solve by hand, such as 2^x = 10.

The method is always the same: put the left side in as y1, the right side as y2, and read the intersections. You can also move everything to one side and find the x-intercepts of a single graph. Both give the same answers, and checking by substitution takes a few seconds.

Graphing gives approximate answers when the solution is not a nice number, so round sensibly and check your answer in the original equation. The examples below show a quadratic, an exponential and an absolute value equation.
points: Graph each side of the equation as its own equation.
The x-coordinates of the intersections are the solutions.
Or move everything to one side and read the x-intercepts.
Always substitute back to check.
